# Andy Whyte Journal: full text

Andy Whyte is the founder and CEO of MEDDICC and the author of the best-selling book MEDDICC. Twenty years in sales. Keynote speaker at sales kickoffs and revenue summits. This file holds the full text of the journal and its reference pages.

## The Maxims

### AWJ No. 01: A-Players Are Uncomfortable Being Comfortable
Pillar: sales. URL: https://andywhyte.com/journal/a-players-are-uncomfortable-being-comfortable/

A-Players are Uncomfortable Being Comfortable.
  They are driven by an unreasonable, unforgiving, and unrelenting mandate to achieve the best version of themselves.
  They are only satisfied when moving at full pace toward their own potential.
  Stagnation is pain.
  The commitment is uncomfortable. The hunger. The constant, nagging&hellip; The toll of asking: "Am I doing enough?" The Impostor Syndrome. The demand for feedback.
  But replace it with comfort, and they'll become uncomfortable.
  Because A-Players are Uncomfortable Being Comfortable.

A decision that defines the maxim

In September 2014, Roger Federer was 33 years old and had won 17 Grand Slams. He had nothing left to prove and a young family at home. Yet he decided to hire a new coach, Stefan Edberg, to rebuild his attacking game and backhand.

He chose to be bad at something in public, in his thirties, after he had already won everything available to win.

He went on to win three more majors after the age of 35.

  
  
    01
    
      Federer and Edberg, French Open 2015. The decision to be a beginner again at 33.
      Photo: Frédéric de Villamil &middot; CC BY-SA 2.0
    
  

Federer sabotaged comfort in pursuit of finding a higher output.

That decision is the maxim. A-Players are uncomfortable being comfortable.

The mistake people make is thinking discomfort is the price of greatness.

It is not the price.

It is the by-product of a mind that demands more.

A mind that knows their career's true potential and psychologically blackmails them to strive to be more, never resting until they meet their potential.

But potential is always one stride ahead.

A-Players know this in their body. They feel suspicious of ease. They feel ill at the idea of easy.

Audit your comfort

What is the thing you are best at?

The thing other people praise you for?

Where on that skill have you plateaued?

Where are you just running the same play because it works?

How do you unlock the next level?

Seek out the discomfort between where you are and where your potential knows you can be.

Embrace the discomfort to fuel you to your next level.

If you are an A-Player, you won't find comfort again until you've uncovered the next level of discomfort.

As such, A-Players are locked in a perpetual growth cycle.

And they'd never have it any other way.

  Reflect
  Do you see yourself in this maxim?
  Are you stuck in a perpetual growth cycle where comfort feels uncomfortable?
  Would you change it?

### AWJ No. 02: Feedback is like Milk. It is Best Served Fresh.
Pillar: founder. URL: https://andywhyte.com/journal/feedback-is-like-milk-it-is-best-served-fresh/

"Feedback is like Milk. It is Best Served Fresh.", Faith Meyer
  My biggest failure as a leader was how bad I was at giving critical feedback.
  It was the main reason I enlisted a coach.
  One of my failings was that I would procrastinate about giving critical feedback.
  I'd tell myself I was waiting for the perfect moment.
  I'd tell myself that I was gathering context to give better feedback.
  But I wasn't doing anyone any favours by doing that.
  It was in these shenanigans that led Faith to come up with the metaphor that feedback is like milk, it's best served fresh. It only sours with time.
  Obviously, there is a time and a place, but if you believe (as you should) that feedback is a gift, then you should prioritise finding the time and place to give feedback.
  Because "Feedback is like Milk. It is Best Served Fresh."

The conversation I should have had a year earlier

My biggest failure as a leader was avoiding the conversations that mattered most.

I had a CXO who was failing. The team saw it. I saw it. Instead of looking him in the eye and telling him the truth, I stayed silent. I told myself I was being patient. I told myself I was being supportive. I told myself I was gathering context.

I was being a coward.

The silence festered. He did not just resign. He raised a grievance against the company.

That failure did not happen because I didn't know how to speak. It happened because I didn't have the guts or the tools to lead.

It is what pushed me to hire a coach. Faith Meyer is the person who finally named the pattern. After watching me dance around a difficult conversation for the third or fourth time, she said, "Andy. Feedback is like milk. It is best served fresh."

The line landed because it described, exactly, what I had been doing wrong.

Delay turns a behaviour into an identity

The reason delayed feedback fails is not that it lacks data. The data was there on day one. The reason it fails is that delay quietly converts a behaviour into an identity.

On Tuesday, your rep ran a bad discovery call. By the following Monday, your rep is someone who runs bad discovery calls. The first version of the conversation is a coaching note. The second is a performance issue.

The same dynamic eats marriages, friendships, and exec hires. Small, specific things go unnamed. They compound. By the time you finally raise them, you are not arguing about the original behaviour. You are arguing about the pattern, the silence, and the resentment that grew in the gap. The original five-minute conversation is now a forty-minute fight. The other person is right to feel ambushed.

Three frames make this trap operational

The first is the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve. People lose roughly half the context of a moment within 24 hours.1 By the time you find "the right time," your colleague cannot accurately reconstruct the moment you are describing. You are now both arguing about a memory, not a behaviour.

The second is loss aversion. Kahneman and Tversky showed that we feel near-term social discomfort far more sharply than diffuse future cost.2 So we delay. The math is wrong, but the feeling is real. Naming the bias is the first step to overriding it.

The third is compounding. Feedback debt accrues interest. The interest is paid in repeated mistakes by the same person. Charlie Munger's frame is sharp here: avoid stupidity before seeking brilliance.3 Most "stupidity" inside teams is a delayed correction.

The right counter-question is not "when is the right time to give this feedback?" That question protects your comfort. The right counter-question is: "what is the cost of waiting one more week?" That question reveals the bill.

Fresh is not the same as raw

This is the part most people miss. John Gottman's work on emotional flooding shows that when the giver is hot, the feedback lands worse.4 Fresh means before the moment cools. Not before you have cooled. The window is short. It is not zero. If you cannot speak without your voice shaking, wait an hour. Not a week.

The strongest counter is: half-baked feedback is worse than no feedback. Sometimes you genuinely need to gather context.

The honest test is this. If you can name precisely what you need to learn before you can speak, and the answer is something you can learn within 24 hours, the delay is justified. If the honest answer is "I just want to feel more sure," you are procrastinating.

The move in that case is to give the partial feedback now, name it as partial, and invite their side. "Here is what I noticed. Here is what I do not know yet. Help me understand." That is fresh feedback that respects complexity. Silence does not.

The 48-hour rule

One practical rule.

If you notice something worth feeding back on, you have 48 hours to either say it, book the time to say it within the next five working days, or decide formally that it is not worth saying. Anything else is procrastination dressed as judgment.

The version of you that gives feedback inside 48 hours has better-performing reps, longer-tenured exec hires, and harder-edged friendships that survive disagreement. The version of you that waits ends up paying the bill in a meeting room where the conversation is no longer about the behaviour. It is about the year of silence.

The price of delayed feedback is always paid. The only question is whether it costs you five minutes or twelve months.

Feedback is like milk. It is best served fresh.

  
    
  
  
    The Coach
    Faith Meyer
    Faith is a former CEO and COO with over two decades of leadership experience. Today she is a coach for the world-class coaching institute Mochary Method, led by legendary CEO coach Matt Mochary, where they help the world's best startup operators, Sam Altman at OpenAI, Brian Armstrong at Coinbase and Naval Ravikant at AngelList among them, unlock their full potential.
    Faith's coaching profile →

    Ebbinghaus, H. (1885). Über das Gedächtnis: Untersuchungen zur experimentellen Psychologie (Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology). Duncker &amp; Humblot, Leipzig.     Kahneman, D., &amp; Tversky, A. (1979). Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk. Econometrica, 47(2), 263&ndash;291. https://doi.org/10.2307/1914185. &#8617;

### AWJ No. 03: The B in B-Player Stands for ‘Busy.'
Pillar: founder. URL: https://andywhyte.com/journal/the-b-in-b-player-stands-for-busy/

The B in B-Player stands for "busy."
  A-Players focus on outcomes.
  They want clear goals and thrive on challenge, accountability, and measurable outcomes.
  They measure success by impact, not appearance.
  B-Players focus on optics.
  They avoid clarity and dodge accountability.
  They fear exposure, resist change, and play it safe to stay liked and in control.
  Their energy goes to managing perception, not creating value.
  Busyness used to be camouflage for B-Players, but in the age of AI, the lights are on, and the differentiator isn't effort, it's initiative.
  Gone are the days when signalling busyness is a badge of honour.
  Today, it's the opposite: if you're not automating, delegating, or eliminating tasks, you'll look like a Luddite, not a legend.
  B-Players are not competing with coworkers anymore. They are competing with machines and the humans who know how to use them.
  It is not about how hard you work. It's about how you measure and communicate your impact.
  A-Players don't talk about how busy they are because it's a moot point. They manage their schedules in accordance with their energy and bandwidth, and prioritise impact.
  A-Players don't talk about how busy they are the same way Jordan, Williams, Hamilton, Messi, and Biles don't talk about how long they spend on the court, gym, simulator, or track. They talk about the impact. The wins. The championships, titles, and medals.
  Am I wrong? Is there someone you class as an A-Player who talks about how busy they are?
  If the B in B-Player stands for "busy," then what does the A in A-Player stand for?

What the A Stands For

A pipeline review last week. The AE has 27 open opps, all yellow or red. He defends every single one with the same line. "I'm working it hard."

He is working it hard. He is also the lowest performer on the team.

The B-Player tell isn't laziness. It's effort displayed as evidence.

The B in B-Player stands for busy. That post landed because most operators recognise the type. The deeper question is why this pattern survived for so long, and why it is finally breaking.

Why busyness worked for so long

It survived because outcomes were expensive to measure and effort was cheap to observe. So organisations measured what they could see. Hours at the desk. Calls dialled. Emails sent. Meetings booked. Slides built. The proxy became the metric. The metric became the goal. Goodhart's Law in slow motion.1

For most of working history, this was a tolerable trade. You couldn't read every commit. You couldn't watch every customer call. You couldn't quantify the quality of a strategy doc. So you rewarded the visible inputs and prayed the outputs followed.

The B-Player figured this out early. They optimised for the visible. They built careers on activity that looked dispositive but wasn't. They kept moving, so no one could ask what they had moved.

The work just got legible

That trade is ending. Not because management got smarter. Because the work got legible.

Every commit is in Git. Every deal stage is in Salesforce. Every customer interaction is in Winni Calls. Every doc edit is timestamped. Every Linear ticket has a velocity. The cost of measuring outcomes has collapsed. The cost of fabricating effort has not.

Bolt AI onto this stack, and the asymmetry sharpens. Anyone with an LLM and ten minutes can ship the deliverable that a B-Player would have stretched across three days. The 9 am meeting brief. The first-draft proposal. The competitor analysis. The board update. The work that used to fill calendars is now a single prompt.

A calendar full of "work" is starting to look like an admission, not a defence.

Reverse the question

The useful move is to reverse the question. Forget "how do I become an A-Player." Ask "what behaviours are now unmistakably B-Player, and how do I stop doing them this week?"

A short list.

Talking about how busy you are. The lights are on. The room can see your output. Reporting hours is reporting the input cost. No one asked.

Defending stalled deals with effort verbs. Worked, chased, pushed, nurtured. Activities, all of them. None of them are MEDDPICC. If you cannot articulate the Champion's economic case in three sentences, the deal is not real, and the effort was theatre.

Owning meetings instead of decisions. The B-Player schedules a meeting to "align." The A-Player writes a one-page memo, names the decision, names the deciders, and books the meeting only if the memo creates disagreement.

Hoarding tasks AI can do. Draft summaries. First-pass research. Comparison grids. Status updates. If you spent the morning on any of those, you spent it competing with a machine for the boring half of your job. The machine wins on cost.

Performing thoroughness. Forty slides when six would do. Three frameworks when one would land. Optics is the tell.

The shift underneath the list

The shift underneath the list is the one that matters. The B-Player believes the job is to be valuable. The A-Player runs the job as if value has to be proved on a single page every Friday. One paragraph on outcomes shipped. One paragraph on what was killed. One paragraph on what's next and why.

Most people will not do this. Writing one page is hard. Running ten meetings is not. The page exposes the week. The meetings hide it. Exposure is the point.

So what does the A stand for?

Not "ambitious." Not "achiever." Both are flattery dressed as identity.

The A stands for accountable. To the outcome, not the activity. To the impact, not the calendar. To a small set of measurable wins, defended in writing, on a regular cadence.

Accountability holds up in daylight because it was built for daylight. Busyness was built for the dark.

This week, run the test on yourself. Open your calendar. Strike out every block that exists to be seen rather than to produce. If half the week disappears, you are closer to the truth than you were on Monday.

Then write the page.

Citations

  
    Goodhart, C. A. E. (1975). Problems of monetary management: The U.K. experience. Papers in Monetary Economics. Reserve Bank of Australia. Popularised by Marilyn Strathern (1997) as: "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." &#8617;

### AWJ No. 04: There is no such thing as a C Player.
Pillar: founder. URL: https://andywhyte.com/journal/there-is-no-such-thing-as-a-c-player/

There is no such thing as a C Player.

Or at least, there shouldn’t be.

You’re either an A Player or you are a B Player, with or without the potential to be an A Player.

Professional sports teams wouldn’t have any space for C Players, so why should your GTM team?

This lens does require two considerations:

1️⃣ Your A Player rating is relative to the level of your role. For example, you could have a junior and senior AE who are both A Players. The junior AE with 1 year of experience isn’t going to be as strong as the senior AE with 10+ years of experience.

You rate them relative to their position.

2️⃣ Being an A Player is subject to form.  There’s literally a phrase for it: ‘Bringing your A game.’

Even the greatest performers can fall out of form.

This is why a critical part of creating the environment for a winning team is to create a place where A Players can thrive.

Help the A and B+ Players in your team to thrive by:
🔋 Focusing on their growth: empowering their growth mindset with a roadmap

🔋 Removing barriers that slow them down (𝙐𝙣𝙥𝙤𝙥𝙪𝙡𝙖𝙧 𝙤𝙥𝙞𝙣𝙞𝙤𝙣: 𝘵𝘩𝘦 ‘𝘣𝘢𝘳𝘳𝘪𝘦𝘳𝘴’ 𝘵𝘦𝘯𝘥 𝘵𝘰 𝘣𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘉− 𝘗𝘭𝘢𝘺𝘦𝘳𝘴)

🔋 Enthusing them with recognition and rewards (𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘫𝘶𝘴𝘵 $$$)

There is obviously a great deal of depth to each of the above, but it’s not overly complicated.

Yet, one thing I don’t think we discuss enough is how disproportionately leaders focus their time on the non-A players in their team.

If leaders were forced to profile their team:
• A Player: 🥇.
• B+ Player: has potential to be an A, 𝗢𝗥 is out of form.
• B− Player: does not have the potential to be an A.

How much of their time is w̶a̶s̶t̶e̶d̶ spent on the B− Players? 🤔

### AWJ No. 05: Failure and invention are inseparable twins
Pillar: founder. URL: https://andywhyte.com/journal/failure-and-invention-are-inseparable-twins-jeff-bezos/

Failure and invention are inseparable twins. Jeff Bezos said it first.

Not going to lie…

This one is ironic.

I love the notion of breaking a concept down into a maxim and have been capturing my favorites in a notebook.

The idea was that I’d have a purpose-created small notebook to remind me of my favorite maxims.

In my head, I’d have this perfect book of maxims in order… Yet I accidentally skipped a page.

1, 2, 3, 5, 4 🙈

I thought I could fix it with a maxim from Bezos about failure.

It would be sweetly ironic.

Then, when writing it out, I made a spelling mistake.

Perfect 😂.

### AWJ No. 06: Authenticity is the Most Intangible Invaluable Interest You Can Have
Pillar: human. URL: https://andywhyte.com/journal/authenticity-is-the-most-intangible-invaluable-interest-you-can-have/

I just got back from a few days in the South of France, and I was struck by how little authenticity I saw.

By the pool, people would show up, strip down, stage an iPhone photoshoot, and leave, without ever enjoying the sun or the water.

Outside Louis Vuitton, queues formed not to shop, but to capture the perfect “walking by” shot for their followers.

What shocked me most wasn’t the posing itself, but the effort to make it all look unplanned, re-shot again and again until it looked “natural.”

The lack of authenticity was staggering. Who are they trying to fool?

Has authenticity lost its value, or have people just stopped caring? 🤔

I don’t think it’s either. Authenticity has always been the highest-value asset… It’s just intangible. And in today’s world, egos crave tangible validation: likes, views, clicks.

The problem? Inauthenticity doesn’t create advocacy or loyalty. The moment the stream of ego-driven content dries up, so does the audience.

On LinkedIn, the same thing happens. It’s not staged photos but the self-congratulatory headlines: “I took the company from $x to $xxx” (as one of hundreds) or claiming to be the savior of their industry.

If there were a way to measure the long-term cost of inauthenticity, I bet many would stop and choose the harder, but more sustainable path: being their true selves.

Yet, unfortunately, I don’t think we’ve hit peak nonsense yet. 🤦‍♂️

So, instead of posting the shot of me sipping the perfect rosé in my swimming trunks that I know you all want (🤥), here’s a Maxim I think of a lot to stay aligned with genuine authenticity 🙅‍♂️📸🩲:

### AWJ No. 07: Your Mental Health is not Linear
Pillar: human. URL: https://andywhyte.com/journal/your-mental-health-is-not-linear/

Your Mental Health is not Linear.

Suicide is the leading cause of death for men under 50.

And several different data sources suggest that a major reason for this rate being so high in men is due to a ‘communication gap,’ with the rationale being that men are less likely to communicate their struggles.

I believe a big contributing factor is the belief that mental health is tied directly to circumstances, that your emotional state should neatly match how “good” or “bad” your life looks.

Society reinforces this idea, yet evidence shows otherwise: people who appear to “have it all” still suffer deeply, and sometimes tragically.

The problem is that this doesn’t make sense on the surface, so people don’t talk about it. Especially men.

We convince ourselves our feelings aren’t valid unless our circumstances are “bad enough.” And so we stay silent.

I only realised this truth because of an extreme circumstance:

In 2018, I had cancer. It sucked. But thanks to the incredible NHS, I recovered.

Not long after, I got a new boss… and without going into details, they were bad, 𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗟 𝗕𝗔𝗗.

Strangely, I found myself more depressed in that situation than I had been facing a potentially life-threatening disease.

Which I know makes no sense.

But that’s how I felt.

And you can’t control how you feel.

Looking back, I see it as a gift. Because it taught me this truth: your mental health is not linear.

Just because your circumstances don’t “seem that bad” doesn’t mean your feelings aren’t real.

And here’s the danger: when we believe they should be linear, we convince ourselves we don’t have the “right” to feel bad, and so we don’t talk.

We bottle it up.

And for too many men, that silence is fatal.

That’s why recognising your emotions, without minimising or suppressing them, is so important.

Because only then can you take the steps that help you feel better.

So the next time you’re feeling low, remember: your emotions don’t need to be justified by your circumstances. They are real, valid, and deserving of your care.

Sometimes all you need is four words: “Fancy a pint, mate?”

Be kind to yourself, friends.

🫶

### AWJ No. 08: Take. Take. Mistake. Cut. Direction. Retake.
Pillar: founder. URL: https://andywhyte.com/journal/take-take-mistake-cut-direction-retake/

𝗧𝗮𝗸𝗲. 𝗧𝗮𝗸𝗲. 𝗠𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲. 𝗖𝘂𝘁. 𝗗𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻. 𝗥𝗲𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲.

Life’s made of takes.

A mistake isn’t failure.

It’s feedback.

What matters is how you respond when the scene cuts.

Surround yourself with those who’ll give you direction.

Be coachable enough to adopt it.

So when it’s time to retake, you ace it.

### AWJ No. 09: Authenticity is felt, not found.
Pillar: human. URL: https://andywhyte.com/journal/authenticity-is-felt-not-found/

Authenticity is felt, not found.

Oxford University ran an experiment.

They scanned people’s brains while showing them Rembrandt paintings.

But there was a trick!…

Some were genuine.

Some were fakes.

…and the participants didn’t know which was which.

When people believed they were looking at a real Rembrandt, their brains lit up 🤩.

When they thought it was a fake, their brains stayed flat 😑.

But as you have probably guessed, sometimes the “authentic” ones were actually fake and vice versa.

The only thing that changed was the story people were told.

The perception of authenticity matters more than the authenticity itself. It’s the meaning we attach that gives feeling.

That’s why this maxim holds true:
𝗔𝘂𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗶𝘀 𝗳𝗲𝗹𝘁, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱.

You can’t manufacture authenticity. Regardless of bold claims you may make or certifications you may have.

It’s belief that defines authenticity and how the person inherently feels.

So whether you’re building a brand, creating, or leading a team, remember:

Authenticity lives in the hearts and minds of others, not just in the facts they find.

### AWJ No. 10: Imposter Syndrome ≡ Self-Awareness
Pillar: human. URL: https://andywhyte.com/journal/imposter-syndrome-self-awareness/

“Imposter Syndrome ≡ Self-Awareness”

Only the self-aware suffer from imposter syndrome.

Everyone I’ve spoken to about this observation agrees.

But I feel like this focuses too much on the ‘syndrome’ and not the ‘imposters’ that cause it.

I am 𝗡𝗢𝗧 talking about people with imposter syndrome, as the imposters…

I’m talking about the 𝗔𝗖𝗧𝗨𝗔𝗟 imposters who are the reason self-aware people get imposter syndrome.

Because, without 𝗔𝗖𝗧𝗨𝗔𝗟 imposters, those out there overselling themselves, claiming success they didn’t authentically achieve, and bigging themselves up beyond their worth, there would be no Imposter Syndrome.

Think about it…

When you feel imposter syndrome, you worry that people are judging you negatively…

💁‍♂️ “𝙒𝙝𝙤 𝙙𝙤𝙚𝙨 𝙝𝙚 𝙩𝙝𝙞𝙣𝙠 𝙝𝙚 𝙞𝙨?…”

💁‍♂️ “𝙃𝙚 𝙨𝙝𝙤𝙪𝙡𝙙𝙣’𝙩 𝙗𝙚 𝙞𝙣 𝙩𝙝𝙞𝙨 𝙧𝙤𝙤𝙢…”

💁‍♂️ “𝘾𝙡𝙚𝙖𝙧𝙡𝙮, 𝙝𝙚’𝙨 𝙤𝙪𝙩 𝙤𝙛 𝙝𝙞𝙨 𝙙𝙚𝙥𝙩𝙝…”

But you only think that because you know it’s what people think about 𝗔𝗖𝗧𝗨𝗔𝗟 imposters.

Not you!

By virtue of you having imposter syndrome, you are actually not an imposter. It wouldn’t be a syndrome if you were…!

As a self-aware person, you only get imposter syndrome when you are growing.

It’s the uncertainty of growing into uncharted territory of your potential that brings on the imposter syndrome…

And that’s Okay. As long as you are kind to yourself and don’t let it hold you back.

Your imposter syndrome is a skill. A strength. An indicator of your emotional intelligence.

And in this ever-inauthentic world, where unearned egos go unchecked, your authenticity will become your number one intangible asset.

P.S. Does anyone else’s spelling go out of the window when you are concentrating on your handwriting? 🤦‍♂️

### AWJ No. 11: Urgency is an emotion. Not a message.
Pillar: sales. URL: https://andywhyte.com/journal/urgency-is-an-emotion-not-a-message/

Urgency is an emotion. Not a message.

I’ve lost count of how many times I’ve heard sales leaders lament a “lack of urgency.”

But urgency is an emotion.

You can’t email an emotion.

You can’t tell people to be urgent.

Urgency must be created.

It’s built on how leaders behave.

True urgency is a determination that every moment matters.

It creates energy that creates focus.

It forces people to shed low-priority work.

It laughs in the face of complacency.

It plays to the watch, not the calendar.

It is not panic. It is not performative busyness. It has no time for appearances.

Nobody can teach you how to be urgent.

But there are requirements:

There must be a genuine truth in the urgency.

There must be consistency in the urgency.

There must be clear communication surrounding the urgency:
• The consequences of being ‘un-urgent’ must be clear.
• The goal/endpoint of the urgency must be clear.
• Everyone’s commitments must be clear. There is no room for vague expectation.

And above all else, urgency must be authentic.

### AWJ No. 12: Nobody Regrets Qualifying Out
Pillar: sales. URL: https://andywhyte.com/journal/nobody-regrets-qualifying-out/

“Nobody Regrets Qualifying Out”

Initially, a phrase I coined to encourage salespeople that qualifying out was not something they’d regret doing.

Either they were right, and the opportunity wasn’t worth pursuing, or qualifying out would correct the customer’s behavior and result in them treating the engagement with more respect.

But as time has gone on, I’ve noticed the maxim applies to much more than just sales.

I’ve not regretted qualifying out of parties I didn’t want to go to.

I’ve not regretted qualifying out of ‘friendships’ I felt weren’t genuine.

I’ve not regretted qualifying out of a job with a bad manager.

What have you not regretted qualifying out of?

### AWJ No. 13: Arrogance is only a strength at holding back growth
Pillar: human. URL: https://andywhyte.com/journal/arrogance-is-only-a-strength-at-holding-back-growth/

A Seller finishes the year at 140% of target and walks into the January kick-off a different person. He stops filling in the MEDDICC fields because he knows his deals. He skips the call reviews because he has heard it all before. He interrupts the new VP in her first meeting to explain how this market really works. By June he is at 30% and telling anyone who will listen that the territory changed.

The territory did not change. He did.

I have watched that arc more times than I can count in twenty years of selling, and I have been the man in it. Never at 140%, sadly, but the mechanics were identical. A bit of success arrived, I decided it was proof of who I was, and I stopped taking anything in.

Arrogance feels like strength from the inside. It feels like certainty. It feels like finally not needing anyone. That is the trick of it, because what you are actually feeling is a door shutting.

What arrogance is good at

Growth only ever arrives from outside you, and it comes through three doors. Feedback, which is somebody telling you something you did not want to hear. Failure, which is reality telling you the same thing less politely. And being a beginner again, which is choosing to be bad at something in public so that you can get good at it.

Arrogance locks all three. It hears feedback as an attack. It files failure under bad luck, bad territory, bad quarter. And it will not be a beginner at anything, because the arrogant person's whole position rests on already knowing.

So the Maxim is literal. Arrogance is strong at exactly one thing. It holds back growth with a grip nothing else can match. A lazy person can be shaken out of it. A scared person can be encouraged through it. An arrogant person built the wall themselves and is proud of the brickwork.

Confidence is a different thing, and you need to be able to tell them apart. Confidence is a conclusion drawn from evidence, and it stays open to new evidence. Arrogance is confidence that has stopped taking evidence. Confidence takes the feedback. Arrogance takes offence.

Where it shows up

In a deal, it is the Seller who tells the forecast call that the Economic Buyer's silence is a formality. In a leadership team, it is the VP who has run the same playbook for eight years and calls every idea from the floor naive. In a founder, it is the one who dismisses the new competitor as a toy, twelve months before the toy takes the account.

More than 35,000 people have been through the MEDDICC Masterclass. The ones who get the least from it tell you inside the first ten minutes that they already do all of this. Sometimes they do. They still get the least from it, because the day was never going to get past the door.

The cruel part is that arrogance usually arrives with a track record attached. You earned the right to be sure. That is what makes it so hard to spot in yourself: the evidence for your certainty is real. It is just old.

The audit

Three questions. Answer them honestly and you will know where you stand.

When did you last lose an argument with someone junior to you and say so out loud?

When did you last choose to be bad at something new, somewhere people could see?

When did someone last tell you something uncomfortable about your work, and what did you do about it in the following week?

If the answers are "I can't remember", "nothing recently" and "I explained why they were wrong", you have found the wall. Humility as a pose will not take it down. Reopening the doors will. Ask for the feedback you have stopped receiving. Pick one skill to be a beginner at this quarter. Treat your next failure as information rather than injustice.

The people still growing at fifty were sure of themselves all along. They just never stopped taking the evidence in.

Which door have you shut, and when did you shut it?

### AWJ No. 14: Whether you were created or coded, you were put here to play a role
Pillar: human. URL: https://andywhyte.com/journal/created-or-coded-you-were-put-here-to-play-a-role/

Think about everything that had to happen for you to be reading this. The town you grew up in. The teacher who took an interest, or didn't. The job you took because the other offer fell through. The manager who gave you the territory nobody else wanted. How much of that was accident, and how much of it was design?

I was reading a devotional this morning and it asked a question that stopped me cold. If you truly believed God designed you for a specific purpose, how would you behave differently? What would you attempt? Which problems would you go after?

Then I flipped it.

Forget God for a second. Say none of this is real. Say it is a simulation, and you were coded. Loaded in with specific attributes, dropped into a specific environment, with a specific set of problems placed around you. A character with a role to play.

The answer did not change.

Two worldviews that cannot both be true, and they hand you the same instruction. You are not here by accident. Whether you were created or coded, you were put here to play a role.

Reading the role

The useful part is that both versions give you the same three clues, and you already hold all of them.

Your attributes. The things you are unusually good at, and the things you cannot stop doing even when nobody is paying you to do them. I cannot walk past a badly qualified deal. Twenty years in sales and I still want to ask who the Economic Buyer is at a dinner party.

Your environment. Where you were placed, who is around you, and what you can see from where you stand that other people cannot. The industry you know from the inside. The team you happen to lead. The city you happen to live in.

Your problems. The specific things that are broken in your line of sight. Nobody put them there for someone else to fix. They are in front of you.

Where those three overlap is the role. Attributes you did not choose, an environment you did not pick, and problems you keep bumping into. The overlap is rarely mysterious. If you are honest, you can name it in a sentence, and you have been able to for years.

I wrote MEDDICC because the book I needed did not exist. I had the attribute, which was having learnt the framework the hard way across several companies. I had the environment, which was teams of Sellers who had been told to use MEDDICC and given nothing to read. I had the problem in my lap every Monday. I did not get a sign. I got a problem and a laptop. That book has now sold over 100,000 copies, and the only decision that mattered was accepting that it was mine to write.

What you are waiting for

The devotional question is the one that bites. If you believed you were here on purpose, what would you attempt?

People answer that question in private and then carry on exactly as before. They are waiting for a sign, or permission, or a version of themselves that feels ready. The Seller who knows the Champion is not real but waits for someone else to call it. The founder with the idea written in a notebook from 2019. The person who knows exactly what they should be doing right now and has built a diary that makes sure they never get to it.

You do not need another sign. You do not need permission. However you got here, you got here on purpose, and the role is sitting in the overlap of three things you already have.

So play it.

What is the role you have known about for years, and what have you been waiting for before you play it?

### AWJ No. 15: Authenticity beats deception
Pillar: human. URL: https://andywhyte.com/journal/authenticity-beats-deception/

A Seller on a discovery call gets asked whether the product does something it does not do. There is a half-second pause. Then he says yes, absolutely, there are customers doing exactly that. The call goes well. The deal moves to stage three. Four months later the customer is in the pilot, finds out, and the Champion who put her name on it stops answering emails.

The lie bought four months. It cost the deal, the Champion, and the account for the next five years.

Deception works in the short term, which is exactly why it is dangerous. If it never worked, nobody would do it. Deception wins the call. Authenticity wins the customer. That is the entire argument, and it took me longer than I would like to admit to believe it.

Why deception loses

Sales is a repeated game. The buyer who sat across from you in 2016 is running procurement somewhere else in 2024. The Champion you let down talks to the Champion at the company you are pitching next quarter. In twenty years I have sold to the same people over and over, at different companies, with different titles. They remember.

Robert Axelrod ran computer tournaments in the early 1980s to find the best strategy in a repeated game. The strategies that won were the ones that never cheated first. The clever, deceptive strategies won early rounds and lost the tournament. Nothing about enterprise sales has changed that.

There is also the maintenance cost. A true thing costs you once, when you say it. A false thing has to be defended on every subsequent call, in every proposal, in the pilot, and in the reference call you now have to coach. The deceptive Seller carries a growing stack of positions to protect. The authentic Seller carries nothing.

And the first person a Seller deceives is themselves. Happy ears. The Economic Buyer who is "basically on board" because she smiled. The "not a no, just a not right now." Forecast accuracy is where self-deception goes to be measured, and every leader reading this knows the rep whose 90% commit lands at 40%.

What authentic selling looks like

Authenticity in a deal is a set of things you are prepared to say out loud.

You say what the product does not do before the customer finds out. Their trust goes up, because now they can believe the things you say it does do.

You say "I don't know, I will find out" and then you find out. The same day.

You tell the Champion where the deal is weak. If you cannot be honest with your Champion, you do not have one.

You put the real number in the forecast. Not the number that makes Monday's call comfortable. The one you would bet your own money on.

You stop pretending to be a consultant, a partner, an advisor. You are a Seller. Customers know, and they respect the ones who know it too.

More than 35,000 people have been through the MEDDICC Masterclass, and the hardest shift for most of them is this one. Qualification is honesty applied to a pipeline. Every letter of MEDDICC is a question you can answer truthfully or fudge. The ones who fudge it get a clean-looking CRM and a terrible year.

The test

Before your next customer call, write down the one thing you are currently letting that customer believe that you know is not quite true. The feature that is on the roadmap rather than in the product. The reference who was coached. The "fully committed" sponsor you have never met.

Then decide whether you say it on the call or let it find them.

Deception always gets found. The only variable is who tells the customer. Authenticity beats deception because the customer finds out either way, and the only choice you ever had was whether they heard it from you.

What are you letting a customer believe right now that you would not want them to discover on their own?

### AWJ No. 18: We fight most what we almost are
Pillar: human. URL: https://andywhyte.com/journal/we-fight-most-what-we-almost-are/

The post that wound me up most this year was written by a founder bragging about a 4am alarm, a 90-hour week and a team that matches his energy. I read it twice. I drafted a reply and deleted it. I thought about it in the car. A stranger's post about his alarm clock took an hour of my day.

Then the uncomfortable bit. I know why it landed. I spent most of my twenties believing hours were the score. I have measured my own worth by them more times than I would like to admit, and I have had to unlearn it in public, slowly, over the last decade. He was a version of me with worse timing.

Indifference is the sign of true distance. You do not fight what you have nothing in common with. You ignore it. The things that get under your skin are the things you recognise.

The narrow band

Freud called it the narcissism of small differences. The fiercest hostility runs between groups that are nearly identical, and the gap gets all the attention while the overlap gets none. Watch two sales methodologies argue on LinkedIn. Watch two founders in the same category at a conference. Watch two siblings.

Think of it as a band. Far from you, nothing. You feel no heat about a trait you have never had. Identical to you, nothing again, because you cannot see it. The fight lives in the narrow band in between: the trait you nearly have, the trait you used to have, the trait you have and have not admitted yet.

That is why your strongest reactions are so useful. Your irritations are a map of your own edges. Every disproportionate reaction is pointing at something.

Where it costs you

In a sales team, the manager who is hardest on one rep is usually looking at his younger self. That rep gets the harshest reviews, the sharpest comments in the pipeline meeting, the least patience. Everyone else in the room can see it. The manager calls it high standards.

In a deal, the competitor you obsess over is the one the customer cannot tell apart from you. The one in a different category gets a shrug. The one with the same positioning, the same three slides and the same reference customers gets the whole team's attention and most of the venom. Your anger is telling you the differentiation is missing. That is a positioning problem, and venom will not fix it.

And in how you carry yourself, the trait you mock loudest in others is the one you are least sure you have shed. I have written more than one post taking apart the self-congratulatory LinkedIn headline. I know exactly how the pull works. That is why I can describe it so precisely.

Using it

Next time you feel the heat rise over someone, do two things before you react.

First, measure the reaction against the offence. If a stranger's post has had an hour of your day, the hour is the data. The post was never worth it. Something in you was involved.

Second, name the overlap. Write down the trait that is annoying you, in one line. Then write down when you last showed it yourself. Not whether. When. You will nearly always find a date.

Once you have the date, the fight loses most of its energy. You are no longer defending the border between you and them. You are looking at a trait you share and deciding how much of it you want to keep. That is a question you can work on. Fighting the other person was never going to change anything about you.

The people you are indifferent to teach you nothing. The people you cannot stand are a reading list.

Who do you fight hardest, and what do the two of you have in common?

### AWJ No. 19: You can't coach a lagging indicator
Pillar: sales. URL: https://andywhyte.com/journal/you-cant-coach-a-lagging-indicator/

A one-to-one, second week of the quarter. The rep is at 38% of her number with ten weeks to go. The manager opens with the dashboard, walks through the gap, and closes with the coaching: she needs to get to 100%. She nods. He books the same meeting for next week.

Nothing in that meeting can change the number. The number is a result. Everything that produced it happened weeks or months ago, in discovery calls he did not listen to and deals he did not inspect. He has coached the scoreboard.

Quota attainment, win rate, revenue, average deal size. They all share the same problem. By the time you can see them, the behaviour that produced them is over. You are looking at a photograph of something that already happened. You cannot coach a photograph.

What you can coach

The behaviours that produce the result are visible long before the result is, if you look in the right place. In a deal, that place is MEDDICC.

Has the rep quantified the Metrics with the customer, or is there a vague line about "efficiency" in the CRM? Has she met the Economic Buyer, or is she taking a Coach's word for it? Can she describe the Decision Process with dates and the Paper Process with names? Is the Champion tested, or merely friendly? Each of those is a leading indicator. Each of those can be changed this week. That is what makes them coachable.

The test is simple. Ask two questions about anything you are about to coach. Can the rep change it before the next meeting? Will you be able to see whether she did? If the answer to either is no, you are not coaching. You are reporting.

Attainment fails both questions. A tested Champion passes both.

The trap on the other side

There is a version of this that goes wrong. Some leaders hear "leading indicator" and reach for activity. Calls made, emails sent, meetings booked. Those are early and they are measurable, so they look like the answer. They are a trap. Activity is a leading indicator of effort. It is only loosely connected to revenue, and the moment you coach to it, you get reps who dial for the dashboard. The B in B-Player stands for busy for exactly this reason.

The leading indicators worth coaching are the ones that cause the outcome, which is a smaller set than the ones that merely happen before it. A rep with 400 dials and no Champion is behind. A rep with 40 dials and three tested Champions is ahead. Coach the cause.

Rewrite the meeting

Take the one-to-one from the opening and run it again.

This time the manager leaves the dashboard closed. He opens with her three biggest deals and asks the same questions of each. What did the Economic Buyer say, in their own words, about the pain? When did she last ask the Champion to do something that cost him political capital, and did he do it? What is the next step, and is it in the customer's calendar or only in hers?

Every answer is something she can act on by Friday. Every answer is something he can check the following week. The number will move because the inputs moved. That is the only direction the causality runs.

More than 35,000 people have been through the MEDDICC Masterclass, and the change leaders describe most often afterwards is the shape of their pipeline review. They stopped asking where a deal would land and started asking what was true about it. That is the whole shift. Inspect the deal, and you will never need to shout at the rep.

Find your last three coaching conversations and write down the thing you coached in each one.

Could the rep have changed it that week, and would you have seen it if they had?

### AWJ No. 20: Judge decisions, not outcomes
Pillar: sales. URL: https://andywhyte.com/journal/judge-decisions-not-outcomes/

Two reps, same team, same quarter. The first closes a deal everyone knew should have been qualified out in month one. No Economic Buyer, no Metrics, a Champion who was really a Coach, and a 35% discount in the final week to drag it over the line. It counts. The second qualifies out of a deal in month two because the Decision Criteria had been written by the Competition and the Economic Buyer would not take a meeting. The Competition closes it.

At the kick-off, the first rep is on stage. The second is explaining herself in a one-to-one.

That is how most sales organisations judge, and it is backwards. The first rep made a bad decision and got a good outcome. The second made a good decision and got a bad one. Reward the outcomes and you will get more of the first rep's decisions, and within a year you will have a team that chases luck and hides its process.

Why outcomes lie

Every outcome is a mix of two things: the quality of the decision and the luck that followed. Over a career you can start to tell them apart. On any single deal you cannot. The deal that closed because the Competition's rep left mid-cycle looks identical, on the dashboard, to the deal that closed because you ran it properly.

Poker players have a word for this. Annie Duke calls it resulting: judging a decision by how it turned out rather than by what you knew when you made it. Poker punishes resulting fast, because you play thousands of hands and the luck washes out. Sales punishes it slowly, because you play twenty deals a year and the luck has time to hide.

Nobody regrets qualifying out. I have said that for years and I stand by it. But a leader who praises the lucky close and interrogates the correct qualify-out is training the team to regret it.

Four boxes

Draw a grid. Good decision or bad decision across the top. Good outcome or bad outcome down the side. Every deal lands in one of four boxes.

Good decision, good outcome. The deserved win. Easy to judge, little to learn.

Bad decision, bad outcome. The deserved loss. Also easy, and usually the only box that gets a review.

Good decision, bad outcome. The unlucky loss. The qualify-out that went to the Competition. The honest forecast that missed because the customer's budget was pulled in the last week. Punish this box and people stop telling you the truth.

Bad decision, good outcome. The lucky win. The 35% discount that closed. The sandbagged forecast that was then "beaten". This is the most dangerous box in the business, because nobody examines a win. The bad decision gets rewarded, repeated, and taught to the new hires.

Most organisations only see two of these boxes. They see wins and losses. The grid gives you the other two, and that is where all the learning is.

Judge the decision

The practical move is to judge the decision at the time it is made, with the information available then, and write it down.

For every significant call on a deal, three lines. What I knew. What I chose. What I expected to happen. Qualify out, discount, walk away from the RFP, go over the Champion's head to the Economic Buyer. Three lines, dated.

Then, when the outcome arrives, you have something to judge other than the outcome. Review the lines, not the result. Was that the right call with what was known at the time? If yes and it lost, say so publicly, because the team is watching what you reward. If no and it won, say that too, quietly, to the rep, because the next one will not be lucky.

A leader who does this for a year ends up with a team that makes better decisions, which is the only thing in sales that compounds. Luck does not.

Go back through your wins this year. Which were good decisions, and which were good luck?

## Topic hubs

### MEDDPICC and MEDDICC
URL: https://andywhyte.com/meddpicc/

The qualification framework behind the best-run sales teams in the world, explained by the person who wrote the book on it. What the letters mean, where teams get it wrong, and how I want it used.

Most teams I meet are running MEDDPICC as a form. Eight fields in the CRM, filled in after the meeting, scored by the rep, admired by the manager, and about as useful for forecasting as a horoscope.

I wrote the book on it. I did not write it so you could fill in a form.

MEDDPICC is a set of questions. Each letter is something you need to know about a deal before you can say you understand it. Ask the questions before the meeting and they tell you what to go and find out. Ask them afterwards and they tell you what you missed. The framework only does its job when you are honest about the gaps.

What the letters mean

MEDDIC is the original. Dick Dunkel and Jack Napoli built it at PTC. Six letters, each one a thing you must know about a deal.

Metrics. The quantifiable value the customer gets from you, in numbers they would defend in their own boardroom and in their words rather than yours.

Economic Buyer. The person with discretionary control of the budget. The one who can say yes when everyone else has said no, and no when everyone else has said yes.

Decision Criteria. The formal and informal standards the customer will use to choose. Yours, if you got there first. Your competitor's, if they did.

Decision Process. The steps, the people and the timing between a decision being made and a contract being signed.

Identify Pain, or as I prefer it, Implicate the Pain. Finding the pain is the easy bit. The work is tying that pain to its cost, and your solution to its relief, until the customer can feel what doing nothing costs them.

Champion. A person with power and influence who sells for you when you are not in the room. A Champion wants you to win because your winning helps them win.

MEDDICC adds a second C for Competition. Anyone or anything competing for the same budget, and that includes doing nothing. The competitor I have lost to most often in twenty years never had a sales team.

MEDDPICC adds a P for Paper Process. Legal, procurement, security. The part of the deal that slides a forecast from this quarter into next in the final week, because nobody asked in month one who signs, who reviews, and how long their queue is.

MEDDIC, MEDDICC or MEDDPICC?

Use the longest one. The thinking is identical across all three. The extra letters stop you pretending that Competition and Paper Process are somebody else's problem. Nobody ever lost a deal because they understood too much of it.

One letter I would not add is a third C for Compelling Event. If you need an extra letter for urgency, you have missed the point of three you already have. Pain plus Metrics plus a Champion is urgency. A compelling event is what you get when those three are real. The end of your quarter is not one, and the customer does not care about it.

Checklist or questions?

Here is how the checklist version goes wrong. A deal review, any company, any quarter.

Manager: "Who is the Economic Buyer?"

Rep: "Eve. The CFO."

Manager: "Have we met her?"

Rep: "Charlie says she is fully on board."

Manager: "Right. Green it is."

What that team has is a Champion's opinion of an Economic Buyer. What they have written down is an Economic Buyer. The CRM cannot tell the difference, and by the time the forecast call comes round, neither can the manager.

The questions version runs the other way. Before the next meeting with Charlie, the rep writes down what she knows about each letter and how she knows it. Economic Buyer: named, never met, status second-hand.

That is now the agenda. The meeting exists to get Charlie to put her in front of Eve, or to find out why he will not. The framework has told the rep what to do on Tuesday. That is what it is for.

A checklist measures how confident the rep feels. Questions measure how much evidence the deal has. Only one of those forecasts anything.

Inspect the deal, not the rep

Deal reviews turn into box-ticking because they turn into interrogations. The rep is on trial, so the rep defends. Worked, chased, pushed, nurtured. Effort verbs. None of them are MEDDPICC.

Put the deal on trial instead. Four questions, in order:

1. Do we belong in this deal?
2. Where is the deal strong for us?
3. Where is it weak, and for what reasons is it weak?
4. What actions move it forward?

Run it that way and the rep stops defending and starts thinking, because the review is now helping her win. The leader learns something true about the forecast. If you cannot articulate the Champion's economic case in three sentences, the deal is not real, and no amount of effort makes it real.

Nobody regrets qualifying out

The hardest part of MEDDPICC is what you do when the letters come back empty. I coined "Nobody regrets qualifying out" to give sellers permission to walk, and I have never seen it proved wrong. One of two things happens. Either you were right, and the opportunity was never worth the time, or the customer's behaviour corrects and they start treating the engagement with the respect a real deal deserves.

Twenty years in sales taught me that the deals which hurt were never the ones I qualified out of. They were the ones I kept in the forecast because the form looked full.

Everything above is the thinking. The letter-by-letter detail, with the deals behind it, is in the book, which has sold over 100,000 copies. If you want your team trained and certified on it, that work happens at meddicc.com, where the MEDDICC Masterclass has more than 35,000 graduates. The glossary on this site defines every term.

Now do one thing. Take your biggest open deal. Write the eight letters down the left of a page. Next to each one, write what you know. In a third column, write how you know it.

How many of the eight survive the third column?

### Sales leadership
URL: https://andywhyte.com/sales-leadership/

Deal inspection, forecast calls that find the truth, and what to do with A-Players and B-Players. Twenty years in sales, boiled down to the leadership habits that hold up on the last day of the quarter.

Every forecast call has the same two people in it. The rep who says "commit" and means "hope", and the leader who hears "commit" and writes it down.

Your job is to be neither.

I have led sales teams for most of my twenty years in the job. At Poq I took the team from six to twenty in twelve months. I have also been the leader who wrote "commit" down and paid for it on the last day of the quarter.

What follows is what I learnt. None of it is complicated. All of it is uncomfortable.

Deal reviews that find truth

A deal review that finds the truth has one rule. The deal is on trial. The rep is not.

Put the rep on trial and you get a defence. Worked it hard. Chased. Pushed. Nurtured. Effort verbs, and not one of them tells you whether the deal will close.

A pipeline review I sat in recently had an AE with 27 open opportunities, every one of them yellow or red, defending each with the same line: "I'm working it hard." He was. He was also the lowest performer on the team.

Put the deal on trial and the questions change. Who is the Economic Buyer, and when did we last speak to her? What has the Champion done for us while we were not in the room? What are the Decision Criteria, and who wrote them? Who owns the Paper Process on their side? Every answer is evidence or it is a gap, and the gap is the rep's plan for next week.

A review that finds truth sends the rep away with a to-do list rather than a bruise.

Commit means what?

Forecast accuracy does not come from pressure. Hassling reps on a Monday produces a number that moves again the following Monday.

The number is a lagging indicator. By the time it is wrong, the quarter is over. You cannot coach a photograph. The leading indicators live inside the deal: a Champion who has introduced you to the Economic Buyer, Metrics the customer wrote down themselves, a Decision Process with dates on it, a Paper Process somebody on their side owns. Count those every week and the forecast looks after itself. Count only the number and you are coaching the scoreboard.

Activity is the trap on the other side. Calls made, emails sent, meetings booked. Those are leading indicators of effort, and coaching to them gets you reps who dial for the dashboard.

Two questions sort them. Can the rep change it before the next meeting? Will you be able to see whether she did? Attainment fails both. A tested Champion passes both.

So when a rep says "commit", ask what they know. Commit means the Economic Buyer has agreed, the Paper Process is mapped and in motion, and the Champion has told you when it signs. Upside means the evidence is there but one of those is missing. Everything else is pipeline. Hold those definitions every week and the words start to mean something.

A, B and no C

There is no such thing as a C-Player. Or at least, there should not be. You are an A-Player, or you are a B-Player with or without the potential to become one. Professional sports teams do not carry C-Players, so why should your team?

Two things make that lens fair. First, the rating is relative to the role. A junior AE with a year's experience and a senior AE with ten can both be A-Players. Second, form. "Bringing your A game" is a phrase for a reason, and even the best fall out of it.

The B in B-Player stands for busy. A-Players focus on outcomes. B-Players focus on optics, and busyness is their camouflage.

The lights are on now. Every deal stage is in the CRM, every call is recorded, and anyone with an LLM can produce in ten minutes the deliverable that used to take three days. A full calendar is starting to look like an admission.

A-Players, meanwhile, are uncomfortable being comfortable. That is what one looks like on your team: suspicious of ease, hungry for feedback, slightly ill at the idea of easy.

Now look at where your time goes. Profile the team honestly. A-Players. B-plus Players, who have the potential to be A-Players or are temporarily out of form. B-minus Players, who do not have that potential.

Most leaders spend most of their week on the B-minus Players and then wonder why the A-Players leave. Spend it on the A and B-plus Players instead: a growth roadmap, barriers removed, recognition that is more than money. Unpopular opinion: the barriers tend to be the B-minus Players.

Judge the decision, not the outcome

A rep closes a deal with no Champion and an Economic Buyer she never met. Luck. Another rep loses a deal he ran perfectly, letter by letter, because the customer's budget was pulled. Good decisions, bad outcome.

Reward the second rep. Coach the first. Every outcome is a mix of the decision and the luck that followed, and on a single deal you cannot tell them apart.

So judge the decision at the time it is made, in writing. What I knew. What I chose. What I expected. Three lines, dated. Review the lines when the outcome arrives, and praise the correct qualify-out out loud, because the team is watching what you reward. Good decisions compound. Luck does not.

That includes your own decisions. My biggest failure as a leader was a conversation I avoided for the best part of a year with an executive who was failing. I told myself I was gathering context. He resigned, and then he raised a grievance against the company.

Feedback is like milk. It is best served fresh, and it sours with every week you wait.

A thinking discipline

Sales leadership is a thinking discipline, and the leader's job is to raise the quality of thinking in the room. Reps copy what you inspect. Inspect effort and you get busyness. Inspect evidence and you get qualification. Panic on the forecast call and you get sandbagging. Show calm, consistent, truthful urgency and you get a team that plays to the watch, not the calendar.

More than 35,000 people have been through the MEDDICC Masterclass. The change leaders describe most often afterwards is the shape of their pipeline review: they stopped asking where a deal would land and started asking what was true about it.

One habit holds it together. One page, every Friday, from every person on the team, including you.

A paragraph on what shipped, a paragraph on what was killed, a paragraph on what is next and why. Writing one page is hard. Running ten meetings is easy. The page exposes the week, which is the point.

The deal review questions, the commit definitions and the Friday page are written up as frameworks on this site, and the thinking behind them is in the book.

Take one deal from this week's commit. Ask five questions about it, none of which contain an effort verb. What do you actually know?

### Keynote speaking
URL: https://andywhyte.com/keynote-speaking/

Keynotes and sales kickoff sessions built around your deals, from the author of MEDDICC. What I speak about, what a good SKO keynote does and does not do, and how I prepare.

The first stage I stood on was at Potters, a holiday resort, in 2001. Entertainer and DJ, three years before I sold anything. You learn fast in that job what a room feels like when it is with you, and the exact moment it leaves. Twenty years of selling later, that is still the only metric I care about on a stage.

Most sales kickoff keynotes lose the room by the third slide. A speaker who has never carried a number tells a team that has to carry one how to feel about it. The team claps, goes to the bar, and sells on Monday exactly the way they sold on Friday.

A keynote has one job. Monday has to be different.

What I speak about

Four things, and they overlap.

Qualification. MEDDPICC, from the person who wrote the book on it and runs the company that teaches it. What the letters mean, where teams fake them, and what the framework looks like when it is a way of thinking rather than a form in the CRM.

Deal inspection. How leaders run deal reviews and forecast calls that find the truth. Why "I'm working it hard" is a confession. Why the B in B-Player stands for busy, and why there is no such thing as a C-Player.

Sales as a thinking discipline. The habits of A-Players, who are uncomfortable being comfortable, and the patterns that separate them from theatre.

The human side of selling. Imposter syndrome, which only the self-aware suffer from. Authenticity, which is felt, not found. Urgency, which is an emotion and cannot be emailed. The things reps carry into the room that no methodology covers.

I speak at sales kickoffs, revenue summits and leadership offsites, in person around the world and virtually.

What a good SKO keynote does

It gives the room one way of thinking they can use on Monday. One. If your team leaves with a framework for their next deal review, you have had a good keynote. If they leave with twelve takeaways and a quote for the wall, they have had a nice morning.

It uses your deals. The best session I can run is built around your team's actual opportunities, your stage gates and the objections your reps hear every week. When the examples are theirs, nobody can dismiss it as theory.

It respects the leaders in the room. Your managers hear their own language in the talk and can carry it into Tuesday's pipeline review without translating.

And it entertains, because people do not act on what bored them.

Now what it does not do. It does not pitch my company. If you want training, that lives at meddicc.com, and the keynote stands on its own.

It does not tell your team they are amazing for an hour, because motivational soundbites fade by Tuesday and your reps know it before you do. It does not recycle last year's deck with your logo on the title slide. And it does not pretend selling is easy. The room is full of people who know it is not.

Three formats

Keynote. A 30 to 60 minute talk built around the MEDDICC framework: the principles, the failure modes, and the patterns that separate A-Players from theatre. For conferences and revenue summits.

Sales kickoff. A bespoke session designed around your deals, your stage gates and your objection patterns. It goes deeper than a keynote because the material is yours.

Master of ceremonies. I host the event end to end. Set the tone, hold the energy, conduct the panels, deliver the close. Best for SKOs and revenue summits, where the day has to feel like one event rather than eight.

How I prepare

I treat every keynote like it has to be the greatest of all time. At MEDDICC we call it the KEYGOAT mindset. Nobody is claiming to be the greatest speaker alive. The standard is for the talk: painstakingly curated, built from scratch for the room, and engineered to send every person out ready to take immediate action.

That starts with your deals. Before I write a word, I want the opportunities your team is working, the stage gates they have to pass, and the objections they keep hearing. I want to know what your leaders inspect and what they let slide. The talk is written from that, which is why no two are the same.

Then it gets rehearsed until the room gets a performance rather than a presentation. The Potters training never left.

Who books me

Sales and enablement leaders at CrowdStrike, Microsoft, Amazon Web Services and Dun and Bradstreet, and at Net Health, MRI Software and Arctic Wolf Networks. Michael Sentonas, President of CrowdStrike, said the session had "incredible passion" and that I "absolutely nailed it". Hannah Klug, VP of Sales Enablement at Arctic Wolf Networks, put it more plainly: "OMG Andy owned the stage!" Susan Kinser at Net Health was grateful that I "flew halfway across the world" to their event. That is the job.

The review I value most came from Adeeb Chowdhury, a sales leader at CrowdStrike, looking back on the half that followed the SKO: "an awesome first half of the FY since SKO". Applause on the day is nice. The half that follows is the point.

If your kickoff or summit is in the diary, tell me about your deals and what your team needs to do differently afterwards. That is where every talk starts.

So. What does your team need to do differently on Monday?

### Imposter syndrome
URL: https://andywhyte.com/imposter-syndrome/

Only the self-aware suffer from imposter syndrome. Where it comes from, why it shows up when you are growing, and why I treat it as a skill: in sales, in founding and on stage.

Only the self-aware suffer from imposter syndrome.

I first wrote that line down as Maxim 10, and I have put it to a lot of people since. Every one of them agreed. But the longer I sit with it, the more I think it looks at the wrong end of the problem. We talk endlessly about the syndrome. We never talk about the imposters.

Who are the imposters?

Not you. The actual imposters. The ones overselling themselves, claiming success they did not authentically achieve, bigging themselves up beyond their worth. The LinkedIn headline that reads "I took the company from $x to $xxx" when there were a hundred other people in the building. Without them there would be no imposter syndrome, because there would be nothing to be mistaken for.

Think about what the feeling actually is. You walk into the room and you worry about what people are thinking. Who does he think he is? He should not be in here. Clearly, he is out of his depth.

You only imagine those sentences because you know they are what people think about actual imposters. You have seen it. You have thought it yourself, about someone else.

So by virtue of having imposter syndrome, you are not an imposter. It would not be a syndrome if you were. The real ones never feel it. That is rather the point of them.

When does it show up?

Only when you are growing. A self-aware person does not get imposter syndrome doing something they have done a hundred times. It arrives at the edge, in the uncharted territory of your own potential, where you cannot yet prove to yourself that you belong. That uncertainty is the feeling. It is also the only evidence you get, in the moment, that you are moving.

A-Players are uncomfortable being comfortable. When I wrote that maxim, imposter syndrome was on the list of discomforts, next to the hunger and the nagging question of whether you are doing enough. Roger Federer hired a new coach at 33, with 17 Grand Slams already won, and chose to be bad at a new backhand in public. You do not do that without feeling, on some Tuesday in practice, like a fraud. He won three more majors after 35.

And that is okay. The two conditions are that you are kind to yourself while it happens, and that you do not let it hold you back. Feel it, name it, walk in anyway.

The first deal, the first team, the first stage

Sales is where I learnt this. Early in my career I felt like I was playing sales on hard mode while everyone around me was on easy mode. The first time I sat across from a real Economic Buyer, someone who could say yes or no to the whole deal, every one of those borrowed sentences ran through my head.

What I know now is that the rep who feels nothing in that room is the one to worry about. The feeling means you understand what is at stake. MEDDIC gave me a way to turn the uncertainty into questions I could go and answer, and the B-Player version of me became the A-Player version. The feeling did not go away. It got a job.

Then the first team. I was a store manager at Phones 4u in 2004 and Head of Sales at Everest Home Improvements before the year was out. Nobody hands you a manual. You are certain the team will work out that you are making it up as you go, and the honest answer is that every first-time leader is.

My biggest failure as a leader came later and had nothing to do with making it up. I avoided a hard conversation with a failing executive for the best part of a year, telling myself I was gathering context, when the truth is I did not yet have the guts or the tools. The feeling had been telling me to go and get the tools. Eventually I listened and hired a coach.

Then the first stage. Mine was at a holiday resort in 2001, as an entertainer and DJ, so I had a head start, and it still did nothing for me the first time I walked out in front of a sales kickoff as the person flown in to tell them how to sell. Founding a company was the same feeling at a larger scale. The first hire. The first time someone introduced me as the CEO and I glanced over my shoulder to see who they meant.

Every one of those firsts had the same signature. New territory, no proof yet, and a self-aware mind filling the silence with other people's imagined verdicts. Every one of them was growth.

Why it is a skill

Your imposter syndrome is a skill. A strength. An indicator of your emotional intelligence. It means you can read a room, see yourself the way others might, and care whether your claims are earned. The actual imposters cannot do any of that, which is exactly why they are so comfortable.

Authenticity is felt, not found. People cannot always say why they trust someone, but they feel the difference between earned and performed, the way the brain lights up for a Rembrandt it believes is real. In an ever-inauthentic world, where unearned egos go unchecked, your authenticity becomes your number one intangible asset.

One honest caveat, because I wrote a Maxim about it. We fight most what we almost are. The self-congratulatory headline winds me up precisely because I know how the pull works, and so do you.

You feel the pull too. The imposter gives in to it. You check your claims against what you actually did before you make them, and that habit is the whole difference. Authenticity beats deception, in a deal and in a career, because the room finds out either way.

The imposters are busy performing. You are busy growing. Over twenty years, only one of those compounds.

So the next time it shows up, do not go looking for a cure. Write down what you are doing that is new. That list is the growth. The feeling is the receipt.

What are you growing into right now?

Twenty years in sales, one book, one company, and a notebook of principles I keep going back to. This page tells you what is here and where to start.

A cobalt reporter's pad. Twenty Maxims, handwritten, one to a page. A Maxim is a single principle cut down until nothing spare is left. Nobody Regrets Qualifying Out. The B in B-Player Stands for Busy. Urgency is an emotion. Not a message. Behind each page sits an essay on where the line came from, usually a deal, a forecast call or a mistake I would rather not have made, and what to do with it.

How to read it

Scroll and the pages flip. Stop on the one that lands, click it, and the essay opens underneath. Then do something with it before you read the next one. Twenty principles skimmed in ten minutes will do nothing for you. One principle applied on Monday will.

Which page are you starting on?

## Landing pages

### MEDDPICC training
URL: https://andywhyte.com/meddpicc-training/

I wrote the book on MEDDICC and founded the company that trains it. This page is what good training looks like, so you can judge any provider against it, mine included.

Most MEDDPICC training fails in the same place. The sessions go well, the slides are good, everyone leaves with a scorecard, and by the third forecast call the team is back to reporting deals instead of inspecting them. The training taught the letters. It never changed the behaviour.

I have sat on every side of this. I spent twenty years selling and leading sales teams, and early on I was playing sales on hard mode while everyone around me seemed to be on easy. Discovering MEDDIC was the turning point. It took me from the B-player version of myself to the A-player version. I wrote the book about it, MEDDICC, which has sold more than 100,000 copies, and I founded the company that built the MEDDICC Masterclass, which has more than 35,000 graduates. The course lives at meddicc.com. This page is my opinion on what good training looks like, written so you can judge any provider against it, mine included.

Who needs it

Anyone selling a deal with more than one decision maker and a procurement process at the end. Account executives running complex deals. The managers who run their forecast calls, because a manager who cannot inspect a deal cannot coach one. Founders selling their own product, who usually need it most and get it last.

The test is simple. Has a rep ever told you a deal is going great? Did you have any way of checking? If not, that is the gap the training fills.

What it should be, and what it should not

Good training does one thing: it changes what a seller does in a live deal.

After it, Metrics are quantified rather than gestured at. The Economic Buyer is named, and met. The Champion is tested: does this person sell for you when you are not in the room, or do they just like you? The Paper Process is mapped before the end of the quarter rather than discovered during it. Competition is named, including the one that wins most often, doing nothing.

Bad training is a checklist with a certificate stapled to it. Eight boxes, ticked. It feels like qualification. It produces the same fiction you had before, better organised, and it hands everyone a shared vocabulary for being wrong. MEDDPICC is a way of thinking about a deal, and you cannot tick your way to a way of thinking.

Bad training also skips the managers. Sellers revert the moment the forecast call rewards the old behaviour, and managers run the forecast call. Train the team without its leaders and you have bought a quarter of good intentions.

What changes when it works

Two things, and you can measure both.

Your forecast gets honest. A forecast is only as reliable as the qualification underneath it. When every deal on the commit line has a quantified Metric, a met Economic Buyer, a tested Champion and a mapped Paper Process, the commit line stops carrying hope. The forecast call turns into an inspection. Do we belong in this deal? Where is it strong? Where is it weak, and why? What moves it forward? Four questions, every deal, every week.

Your team qualifies out. Deals that were never going to close get found early, and the time goes into the deals that can. Nobody regrets qualifying out. The rep gets their quarter back, the customer who was never going to buy gets left alone, and the forecast stops lying.

My position

Go all in or do not start. MEDDICC is binary. You either use it or you do not, and a team that runs it on the big deals and skips it on the small ones has not adopted it. Adoption takes a full sales cycle, because you need deals qualified under the new rules from first meeting to close before the numbers move. Budget for the cycle and inspect every week.

Pick a provider on three questions. Who wrote the content, and have they carried a quota? How are the managers trained? What happens after the sessions end? Thin answers, keep looking.

If you want the methodology explained and argued over, the MEDDPICC hub is where I do that, and the book is the full method, letter by letter. If you want your team trained, go to meddicc.com. If you want me in the room for your kickoff, that is a speaking enquiry.

How many deals on your commit line would survive the four questions?
