A sales keynote has one job: change what the room does on Monday. Most of them fail it. The speaker is funny, the slides are slick, the team claps, and by Tuesday nobody can tell you what they are doing differently. The energy was real. It had nothing to attach to.

I keynote sales kickoffs, conferences and revenue summits, in person worldwide and virtually, for organisations including CrowdStrike, Microsoft, Amazon Web Services and Dun and Bradstreet. ## Frameworks

### MEDDPICC
URL: https://andywhyte.com/frameworks/meddpicc/

Eight questions that tell you whether a deal is real, where it is weak and what to do next.

MEDDPICC is a qualification framework. Eight letters, each one a question you ask about a deal: Metrics, Economic Buyer, Decision Criteria, Decision Process, Paper Process, Implicate the Pain, Champion, Competition. Answer all eight with evidence from the customer and you know whether the deal is real, where it is strong, where it is weak and what to do about it. Leave any of them blank and you are forecasting a guess.

It exists because complex deals fail in predictable places. The original six letters came out of PTC in the 1990s, where Dick Dunkel and Jack Napoli worked out what the won deals had in common that the lost ones did not. The seventh, Competition, was added because sellers kept losing to rivals and to "do nothing" without seeing either coming. The eighth, Paper Process, was added because the stretch between a verbal yes and a signed contract was killing deals on the last day of the quarter. Every letter is a scar.

How to run it

Start with the deal in front of you and write the eight letters down. Against each one, record what the customer has actually said or done, not what you believe. "The CFO is the Economic Buyer" is an assumption until the CFO has engaged. "They want to save money" is not a Metric until there is a number, a baseline and an agreement. Then score honestly. Which letters are proven, which are assumed, which are blank?

The weakest letter tells you the next action. A deal with no Champion needs a Champion built or tested before it needs another demo. A deal with no Paper Process mapped needs that conversation before anyone talks about dates. Do this every week on the deals that count, and let the gaps drive the agenda.

It boils down to four questions. Do we belong in this deal? Where is it strong for us? Where is it weak, and why? What actions will move it forward?

Where it breaks

It breaks the moment it becomes admin. Eight mandatory CRM fields filled in from memory on a Friday afternoon are a form, and a form never closed anything. It breaks when the letters are answered by the seller instead of the customer. It breaks when leaders ask whether the fields are complete instead of asking how we know. And it breaks when teams half-adopt it, running it on big deals only, or in forecast week only, and then conclude it does not work.

MEDDPICC is binary. You use it on everything or you do not use it. Go all in and it pays you back in a forecast you can stand behind. Do it by halves and you get the paperwork without the insight.

### The Champion Test
URL: https://andywhyte.com/frameworks/champion-test/

A short set of asks that proves whether your Champion is real before you forecast on them.

The Champion Test is a model for one of the most expensive mistakes in enterprise sales: forecasting a deal on a person who was never going to sell it for you. A Champion has power and influence, a vested interest in your success, and actively sells on your behalf when you are not there. A Coach likes you, helps you and gives you information. Both are valuable. Only one closes deals. The test exists because, from the outside, they look identical. Both take your calls. Both say encouraging things. The difference only shows up under load.

Why it matters is simple arithmetic. A deal with a real Champion is one you can forecast, because someone inside the building is working it between your meetings. A deal with a Coach is one you are working alone, in a building you cannot enter. Most of the "surprise" losses I have inspected over twenty years were not surprises. The seller had a Coach, called them a Champion, and the deal died in a meeting the Coach could not get into.

How to run it

First, the three criteria, answered with evidence rather than feeling. Power and influence: when this person speaks in a meeting, do decisions change? Vested interest: what do they personally get if we win, and what do they lose if we do not? Actively selling: what have they done for us, without being asked, in the last two weeks?

Second, the ask. Request something with a cost attached. Thirty minutes with the Economic Buyer. The evaluation team's scoring sheet. A straight account of what the Economic Buyer said about you after the last meeting. A slot on the steering committee agenda. Make it specific and give it a date.

Third, watch the behaviour. A Champion finds a way, or tells you plainly why not and what they will do instead. A Coach goes quiet, or explains the politics at length and does nothing. The action is the answer.

Fourth, write it down. "Champion: got us the EB meeting on the 14th" is evidence. "Champion: very supportive" is not.

Where it breaks

It breaks when the ask is too easy, because anyone will forward a document. It breaks when the seller asks "are you our Champion?" and accepts the yes, since nobody has ever said no to that. It breaks when it is run once and never again. People change roles, lose internal battles, and get handed bigger projects. The Champion who passed in month one can be a Coach by month four, and the only way to know is to ask them for something again.

Keep the bar high. A true Champion does not just prefer your product. A true Champion sells it internally when you are not in the room, and the proof is always something they did.

### Qualifying Out
URL: https://andywhyte.com/frameworks/qualifying-out/

A decision rule for walking away from deals that fail qualification, so your time goes where it wins.

Qualifying out is the decision to stop working an opportunity because it fails qualification. It is deliberate, it has a reason you can say out loud, and it is one of the most underused moves in sales. Nobody regrets qualifying out. I coined that line to give sellers permission, and in all the years since I have not found the exception.

It exists because pipeline has a cost. Every hour spent on a deal with no Economic Buyer access, no Champion and no reason to act this year is an hour taken from a deal that has all three. Sellers know this and still hold on, because killing a deal feels like admitting failure and a fat pipeline feels like safety. It is not safety. It is a coverage number that the leadership team is relying on and that will evaporate in the last two weeks of the quarter, when it is too late to replace.

How to run it

Start with the gap, named in MEDDPICC terms. Not "it has gone a bit quiet" but "we have never met the Economic Buyer and the Champion has not been able to get us there in six weeks". Then set one dated action that would close it, and be direct with the customer about what you need. "For this to make sense for both of us, I need thirty minutes with your CFO before the 20th."

If the date passes and nothing moves, decide. Tell the customer, politely and without drama, that you are stepping back until the conditions change. Write the reason down in one sentence so the forecast is honest. Then watch.

One of two things happens, and both are a win. Either you were right, the deal was never going to close, and you have your time back. Or the act of walking away changes the customer's behaviour. The Economic Buyer who could not find a slot finds one. The procurement process that was going to take ninety days takes thirty. The Coach who could not help you finds some power they had been keeping in reserve. People treat an engagement with more respect when they see it can be withdrawn. You cannot bluff this. You have to mean it.

Where it breaks

It breaks when it is used as an excuse. Qualifying out of a hard deal is not the same as qualifying out of a bad one, and sellers who walk away from every deal that needs real work are avoiding, not qualifying. The gap has to be real, named, and tested with an action first.

It also breaks when leaders punish it. If a rep gets shouted at for shrinking their pipeline, they will learn to keep dead deals alive, and the forecast will be fiction again within a quarter. Judge the decision. A clean qualify-out, with the reason stated, is a good decision even when a competitor later wins the account. Reward it as one.

### Deal Inspection
URL: https://andywhyte.com/frameworks/deal-inspection/

A weekly rhythm for examining the deals that matter against MEDDPICC and judging the decisions inside them.

Deal inspection is the discipline of looking into a deal instead of listening to a summary of it. A seller tells you the deal is going great. Inspection asks how we know. Who is the Economic Buyer and when did we last speak to them? What Metrics has the customer agreed, in their words? What has the Champion done for us in the last fortnight? Where is the Paper Process and who owns it on their side? Every answer gets the same follow-up, and the follow-up is the whole method: how do we know?

It exists because a forecast is only as good as the evidence under it, and most forecasts are built on what reps say. Reps are not lying. They are optimistic, they are close to the deal, and they have a quarter to make. A leader who only hears the rep's version is forecasting blind, and the miss, when it comes, is a surprise to everyone except the customer. Inspection is how a leader stops being surprised.

How to run it

First, choose. You cannot inspect forty deals in an hour, so pick the five or six that decide the quarter and go deep. Second, run the letters. MEDDPICC gives you the questions, and the rep's answers go into one of three piles: proven by the customer, assumed by the seller, or blank. Third, find the weakest letter and agree one action that would change it, with an owner and a date.

Fourth, judge the decisions. This is the part that separates inspection from interrogation. The question is never "why is this deal red?". It is "what decision was made that left us without a Champion in week six, and what do we do differently?". You can coach a decision. You cannot coach a result that has already happened.

That last point is the heart of it. Judge decisions, not outcomes. A rep who qualified out of a weak deal made a good decision even if a competitor later closed it. A rep who won without ever meeting the Economic Buyer got lucky, and luck does not scale. Inspection rewards the first rep and asks hard questions of the second, because the first behaviour produces forecasts you can trust and the second produces a quarter that depends on the weather.

Where it breaks

It breaks when it becomes an interrogation. A rep who leaves feeling attacked learns to hide the gaps, and a hidden gap is worse than an open one. It breaks when the leader inspects lagging indicators, shouting at a win rate the rep already knows about instead of coaching the Champion conversation that would change the next one. It breaks when actions are agreed and never followed up, so the same deal appears with the same gap three weeks running.

And it breaks when it is done in forecast week only. Inspection is a rhythm. Weekly, on the deals that matter, with the follow-ups kept. The forecast you can stand behind comes out of that rhythm and nowhere else.

### A, B and C Players
URL: https://andywhyte.com/frameworks/a-b-c-players/

A model for profiling a team honestly and putting leadership time where it compounds.

The model has three parts, and each one is a Maxim. A Players are uncomfortable being comfortable. The B in B-Player stands for busy. There is no such thing as a C Player.

A Players are driven by an unreasonable demand to reach their own potential. They want clear goals, they thrive on accountability, and they measure themselves on impact. Stagnation is pain to them. Roger Federer at 33, with 17 Grand Slams, hiring a new coach to rebuild his backhand in public, is the picture. B Players focus on optics. They avoid clarity, dodge accountability and spend their energy managing perception. The tell is effort displayed as evidence: the AE with 27 open opportunities, all yellow or red, defending every one with "I'm working it hard". He is working it hard. He is also the lowest performer on the team. And C Players do not exist, or at least should not. Professional sports teams have no room for them. Neither does yours.

It exists because leaders put their time in the wrong place. Profile a team honestly and you get A Players, B+ Players who have the potential to be an A or are temporarily out of form, and B- Players who do not have the potential. Most leaders spend a disproportionate share of their week on the B- group. The A Players, who would grow fastest with that attention, are left to get on with it, and the barriers in their way, which are often the B- Players themselves, stay where they are.

How to run it

Profile every person, privately and honestly. Rate them relative to their role: a first-year AE and a ten-year veteran can both be A Players, and the junior one will not be as strong in absolute terms. Allow for form, because A is subject to it, and even the best lose their A game for a quarter.

Then allocate your time. Growth plans and stretch for the As. Clear goals, feedback and a fair window for the B+ group to show which way they are going. A direct conversation with the B- group, early, because feedback is like milk and it sours. Then remove barriers. Ask each A Player what slows them down and fix it.

Where it breaks

It breaks when the labels become permanent. Form changes, people grow, and a B+ who gets the right coaching becomes an A. It breaks when A is confused with loud, senior or busy, which is how B Players get promoted. It breaks when the leader uses it as a sorting exercise rather than a coaching one, because the point of the model is to decide where your time goes, and the answer is almost always more on the As than you are currently spending.

And it breaks when you do not act on the B- conversation. Knowing someone does not have the potential and keeping them anyway is the most expensive kind of comfort, for them and for you.

### Judge Decisions, Not Outcomes
URL: https://andywhyte.com/frameworks/judge-decisions-not-outcomes/

A way of reviewing performance that separates the quality of a decision from the luck in its result.

Judge decisions, not outcomes. Sales is a game of probabilities played with incomplete information, which means good decisions lose and bad decisions win, often enough to fool anyone who only looks at the scoreboard. A rep who forecasts a deal with no Economic Buyer, no Metrics and a Coach they call a Champion, and then closes it because the customer's CFO happened to have budget to burn in December, has made a bad decision with a good outcome. A rep who qualified out of a deal that a competitor later won has often made a good decision with a bad outcome. If you reward the first and punish the second, you are training your team to gamble.

It exists because outcomes are loud and decisions are quiet. The number is on the dashboard. The decision that produced it is buried in a CRM note from eight weeks ago, if it was recorded at all. Left alone, every review drifts towards the result, and results carry luck in them that nobody can coach. Decisions can be coached. They are the leading indicator. The outcome is the lagging one.

How to run it

Take the result and put it to one side. Then go back to the point of decision and reconstruct what was known. In a deal, that means the state of MEDDPICC at the time: which letters were proven, which were assumed, which were blank. Ask what the best available decision was with that information. Was committing the deal reasonable? Was walking away reasonable? Was spending another month on it reasonable? Then compare it to the decision actually taken. Grade that, out loud.

Finally, grade the process that produced the information. A rep who made a sound decision on bad information has a discovery problem, which is a different conversation from a judgement problem.

Then do the uncomfortable part. Praise the good decision that lost, in front of the team. Correct the bad decision that won, in private but clearly. Both feel wrong in the moment. Both are the only way a team learns that the rule is real.

Where it breaks

It breaks when it is used as an excuse. "It was a good decision at the time" has to be earned by showing what was known at the time, and a rep who cannot reconstruct that has not earned it. It breaks when leaders apply it to others and not to themselves. The forecast you called, the hire you made and the territory plan you signed off deserve the same review. It breaks under quarter-end pressure, when a leader who believes in the rule on the first of the month abandons it on the thirtieth because the number is the number.

And it breaks if you drop outcomes entirely. Outcomes still matter. They are the scoreboard, and over a long enough run of decisions they are also the best evidence of whether the decisions were any good. Judge the decisions first. Let the outcomes accumulate.

### Lead on Leading Indicators
URL: https://andywhyte.com/frameworks/leading-indicators/

Pick the few inputs that predict the result and coach those, because the result itself cannot be coached.

You can't coach a lagging indicator. Bookings, quota attainment, win rate, churn: by the time any of those is on a dashboard, the work that produced it is over. Telling a rep they are at 40% of target tells them something they knew before you opened your mouth, and no amount of discussing it changes a single decision that led there. A leading indicator is different. It happens earlier, it predicts the result, and it is still in play. The whole model is choosing to lead on those.

It exists because sales leadership defaults to the scoreboard. Attainment sits at the top of every report, every one-to-one starts there, and the conversation that follows is a post-mortem dressed as coaching. Leaders who run this way spend the quarter shouting at a number. The result shows up ninety days after the behaviour that caused it, and by then the only thing left to do is explain it to the board.

How to run it

Start with the lagging indicators you are measured on and accept that you cannot touch them directly. Then work backwards. What, if it happened more, would make bookings go up? For most teams I have led, the answers were the same few things. The quality of MEDDPICC on the top deals. The number of Economic Buyer conversations in a month. The share of new pipeline that carried a tested Champion. Discovery calls where the consequence of doing nothing was named by the customer. Pick three or four, no more, and put a number on each.

Then change the shape of your conversations. The one-to-one starts with the leading indicators, the coaching is about the next action that moves one of them, and the attainment number is mentioned once, if at all. Over a quarter, the lagging number follows, with a lag you can roughly predict. That lag is the forecast.

Where it breaks

It breaks when you pick activity instead of leading indicators. Calls dialled and emails sent are inputs, and the B-Player will happily give you more of them. A leading indicator has to predict the result, which means it has to carry quality: a Champion who passed the test, a Metric the customer agreed, an Economic Buyer meeting that actually happened. It breaks when the indicator becomes the target and people start gaming it, which is why you check monthly that it still predicts anything. It breaks when leaders keep both dashboards and still coach from the lagging one out of habit.

And it breaks when the board only wants the lagging number and the leader stops showing them the leading ones. Show them anyway. A board that can see Economic Buyer coverage on the top ten deals has a better forecast than one that can see last quarter's attainment. Everyone can see last quarter. The job is to see this one.

## Glossary

### Metrics
URL: https://andywhyte.com/glossary/metrics/

Metrics are the quantifiable measures of the value your solution delivers to a customer, expressed in numbers the Economic Buyer would recognise and sign off against.

Metrics are the numbers that prove your solution is worth buying. Not your product's numbers, the customer's. A 30% shorter sales cycle. Four hours a week handed back to every engineer. A churn rate cut from 8% to 5%. If the figure describes what changes in their business, it is a Metric. If it describes your feature, it is a brochure.

The question Metrics answer is the one the Economic Buyer will ask whether you are in the room or not: what do we get for the money?

The mistake is to treat Metrics as a line you fill in after the demo. Sellers write "efficiency gains" in the CRM and call it done. That is a word, not a Metric. A Metric has a number, a baseline and a timeframe, and the customer has agreed it. The biggest gap I see is between a Metric the seller believes and a Metric the customer has said out loud. Only the second one moves a deal.

Here is how I use them. Metrics are the bridge between the pain you have implicated and the urgency the deal needs. Pain tells the customer something hurts. Metrics tell them how much, and what fixing it is worth. Put the two together with a Champion who will carry the numbers to the Economic Buyer and the deal starts to move. Without them, your proposal is a price with nothing on the other side of the scales.

### Economic Buyer
URL: https://andywhyte.com/glossary/economic-buyer/

The Economic Buyer is the person with final authority over the budget for your deal, who can say yes when everyone else says no.

The Economic Buyer is the one person who can release the funds for your deal. They have discretionary control of the budget, they can veto a decision the rest of the organisation has already made, and they can find money that officially does not exist. Everyone else in the deal is influencing. The Economic Buyer is deciding.

The question this letter answers is simple: who actually signs this off, and have we met them?

The mistake, and I have made it myself, is to accept the first senior person who talks to you as the Economic Buyer. A VP who manages the budget is not the same as the person who owns it. Procurement is almost never it. Your Champion will sometimes tell you they are it, because admitting otherwise feels like admitting they lack power. Ask the question that settles it: if this decision were made today, whose name would be on the approval? If the answer is a committee, keep digging. Committees do not own budgets. People do.

How I use it. In twenty years I have not seen a complex deal close without the Economic Buyer engaged somewhere, either directly by the seller or through a Champion who could get in front of them. So I treat access as a qualification test. If I cannot get to the Economic Buyer, and my Champion cannot either, I ask why. Usually the honest answer is that the deal is not as important to them as it is to me. That is a deal to qualify out, or to fix before it costs me a quarter.

### Decision Criteria
URL: https://andywhyte.com/glossary/decision-criteria/

Decision Criteria are the standards a customer uses to judge which solution to buy, split into technical, business and often legal or commercial requirements.

Decision Criteria are the rules the customer will use to pick a winner. They come in two main flavours. Technical Decision Criteria: does it integrate, is it secure, will it scale, can our people run it? Business Decision Criteria: what does it cost, what does it return, how fast, and what is the risk if it fails? Many deals carry a third set around legal and commercial terms, and those are the ones nobody mentions until week eleven.

The question this letter answers is: on what basis will they choose, and who wrote that basis?

The mistake is to assume the criteria are fixed and fair. They are neither. Decision Criteria are written by people, and in most competitive deals one of your competitors wrote them with the customer months before you arrived. If the RFP asks for a feature only one vendor has, you know who was in the room. Sellers who take the criteria as given spend the whole deal answering someone else's exam paper.

How I use them. First, I find out whether the criteria exist in writing, who authored them, and whether the Economic Buyer agrees with them. Second, I work with my Champion to influence them while they are still soft. If the customer's real pain is a Metric we move and the competition cannot, that Metric belongs in the criteria. Third, I test my own position against them honestly. If we meet six of nine and the three we miss are the ones the Economic Buyer cares about, the colour of the deal in the CRM is red, whatever the rep says.

### Decision Process
URL: https://andywhyte.com/glossary/decision-process/

The Decision Process is the series of steps, people and approvals a customer goes through to arrive at a buying decision, with dates attached.

The Decision Process is how the customer gets from "we should look at this" to "we have chosen". Who evaluates, who validates, who recommends, who approves, in what order, and by when. It covers the proof of concept, the security review, the business case to the board, the vote in the steering committee. Every one of those is a step, and every step has an owner and a date, whether or not anyone has told you what they are.

The question it answers: what has to happen, in what order, for this customer to decide?

The mistake is confusing your sales process with their buying process. Your pipeline stages are yours. The customer does not know they are in "Stage 3: Proposal". They are in "waiting for Priya to come back from leave so she can look at the integration". Sellers who forecast off their own stages are guessing. Sellers who forecast off the customer's Decision Process are reporting.

How I use it. I ask my Champion to walk me through the last time their company bought something like this, step by step. Who was involved, how long it took, where it stalled. Then I write it down and test it with the Economic Buyer, because the Champion's version and the Economic Buyer's version are often different, and the Economic Buyer's is the one that counts. The output is a dated plan the customer has agreed to. That plan, shared and owned by both sides, is what a Mutual Action Plan is. If a step on it slips with no explanation, the close date slips with it. No exceptions.

### Paper Process
URL: https://andywhyte.com/glossary/paper-process/

The Paper Process is every legal, procurement, security and compliance step between the customer saying yes and a signed contract landing in your inbox.

The Paper Process is the part of the deal that happens after the customer has decided to buy you and before you can book it. Legal redlines. Procurement onboarding. The security questionnaire with 214 questions. Data processing agreements. Signature authority, which in some companies means one person and in others means three people in two countries. It is the P that turned MEDDICC into MEDDPICC, and it earned its letter because of how many deals it has quietly killed on the last day of a quarter.

The question it answers: once they say yes, what has to be signed, by whom, and how long does that take?

The mistake is to start asking about it when the verbal is in. By then the clock is already running and you have nothing left to negotiate with. Legal does not care about your quarter end. Procurement has a 30 day onboarding cycle it will not shorten because you asked nicely. The seller who discovers in the last week of March that the customer's standard terms need a 45 day review has not been unlucky. They have been unprepared.

How I use it. I map the Paper Process in discovery, in the same conversation as the Decision Process, and I treat the two as one timeline. Who owns legal review, what their standard terms look like, whether they have bought from a vendor like us before and how long that took. Then every step goes on the Mutual Action Plan with a date and an owner on their side. If the close date in the CRM lands before the Paper Process can physically finish, the close date is wrong, and I would rather know that in month one than on the last day of the quarter.

### Implicate the Pain
URL: https://andywhyte.com/glossary/implicate-the-pain/

Implicating the Pain means going beyond naming a customer's problem to the point where they feel its cost, own its consequences and connect your solution to the cure.

In MEDDIC, the I stood for Identify Pain. In my book it stands for Implicate the Pain, and the difference is the whole game. Identifying pain is noticing the customer has a problem. Every seller on earth can do that in the first call. Implicating the pain is when the customer themselves connects the problem to what it costs them, what it will cost them if it continues, and what fixing it would mean for them personally. Identified pain sits in your notes. Implicated pain sits in their stomach.

The question it answers: why would this customer change anything at all?

The mistake is to stop at identification and start pitching. The seller hears "our reporting is manual" and launches into the dashboard demo. The customer nods, says it looks great, and does nothing, because manual reporting has been annoying for three years and nobody has been fired for it yet. Annoying is survivable. You have to help them see what else is true: the board decision made late on bad data, the two analysts who quit, the forecast miss that followed. Pain without consequence is a feature request.

How I use it. I ask what happens if nothing changes. Then I ask again, one level up, until I reach a consequence somebody with a budget would lose sleep over. That consequence, with a number attached, becomes a Metric. The person who feels it most becomes my Champion. Urgency in a deal is an emotion, the same as it is in a team. You cannot message it into existence. You implicate it, and then the customer brings it to the meetings for you.

### Champion
URL: https://andywhyte.com/glossary/champion/

A Champion is someone inside the customer with power and influence, a vested interest in your success, and who actively sells for you when you are absent.

A Champion has three things. Power and influence in the organisation, which is rarely the same as seniority. A vested interest in your success, meaning a personal win riding on your deal: a promotion, a problem that has been embarrassing them for a year, a project they put their name to. And they actively sell for you. They fight for you in meetings you will never see, and they tell you what the Economic Buyer really said after the door closed.

The question a Champion answers is the one that decides most complex deals: who is selling this when we are not there?

The mistake is to confuse someone who likes you with someone who champions you. The friendly contact who takes every call, loves the product and gives you great information is often a Coach. Valuable, but a Coach has either no power to move the deal or no reason to spend their political capital on it. Sellers write "Champion" next to that name in the CRM because it feels better than writing "nice person, no power". Then the deal dies in a meeting they were not invited to and nobody can explain why.

How I use it. I do not take the title on trust. I test it. I ask the Champion to do something that costs them: get me in front of the Economic Buyer, share the real Decision Process, tell me where we are losing to the competition. Champions do these things. Coaches apologise and explain why they cannot. The deals I regret are the ones where I knew which of the two I had and carried on anyway. Nobody regrets qualifying out of a deal with no Champion. Plenty regret the reverse.

### Competition
URL: https://andywhyte.com/glossary/competition/

Competition is anyone or anything competing for the same budget, attention or decision as your deal, including rival vendors, an internal build and doing nothing at all.

Competition is wider than the vendor whose logo sits next to yours on the shortlist. It is any person, project or option competing for the same money, the same people and the same slot on the Economic Buyer's agenda. The other vendor, yes. Also the internal team who want to build it themselves. The other initiative that needs the same budget this year. And the biggest competitor of all, which beats every seller more often than any rival does: the status quo. Doing nothing is free, familiar and carries no risk of a career-ending mistake. That is a hard opponent.

The question this letter answers: what else could they do with this money, and why would they do it?

The mistake is losing to a competitor you never named. Sellers fill the Competition field with "none" or with the one rival they heard mentioned on the first call. Meanwhile the CFO has a list of eleven things she could fund and your project is number seven. You were never competing with the vendor. You were competing with a warehouse refit.

How I use it. I ask the Champion a direct question: if we did not exist, what would you do? The answer tells me who I am really up against. Then I find out which competitor helped write the Decision Criteria, because somebody usually did. And I work out where each option is stronger than us, honestly, in writing. If the honest answer is that the internal build is good enough and the Economic Buyer trusts the team doing it, the deal is a qualify-out, and I would rather know that in week two than in week twenty.

### MEDDIC
URL: https://andywhyte.com/glossary/meddic/

MEDDIC is the original six-part sales qualification framework, created at PTC in the 1990s, covering Metrics, Economic Buyer, Decision Criteria, Decision Process, Identify Pain and Champion.

MEDDIC is where it all started. Dick Dunkel and Jack Napoli built it at PTC in the 1990s, out of a study of why the company won deals, lost deals, and sometimes never got a decision at all. Six things kept showing up, and they became the letters: Metrics, Economic Buyer, Decision Criteria, Decision Process, Identify Pain, Champion. PTC went on one of the great growth runs in enterprise software with it, and it has been the backbone of serious sales qualification ever since. Dick and Jack were generous enough to write the foreword to my book on it.

The question MEDDIC answers has not changed in thirty years: is this deal real, and what do we not know about it?

The mistake is to treat the six letters as fields to fill in rather than questions to answer. A CRM with every MEDDIC box ticked tells you the rep is good at admin. It tells you nothing about whether the Champion would walk into the Economic Buyer's office for you. The framework is binary. You are either using it to interrogate your deals or you are using it to decorate them.

How I use it. MEDDIC is the base the later variants build on, and I still think of it as the minimum. If a seller cannot tell me the Metrics, name the Economic Buyer, describe the criteria and the process, explain the pain and point to a Champion, the deal is not qualified, whatever stage the pipeline says it is in. Everything that came later, the second C and the P, sits on top of these six. Learn these first.

### MEDDICC
URL: https://andywhyte.com/glossary/meddicc/

MEDDICC is the MEDDIC qualification framework with a second C added for Competition, so sellers qualify who and what they are really up against.

MEDDICC is MEDDIC plus Competition. Seven letters: Metrics, Economic Buyer, Decision Criteria, Decision Process, Implicate the Pain, Champion, Competition. The second C was added because sellers kept losing deals that looked qualified on every other letter, to rivals they had never properly assessed, or to the customer deciding to do nothing at all. Competition was always part of the conversation. Adding the letter made it part of the inspection.

It is also the name of my book, which has sold over 100,000 copies and carries a foreword from Dick Dunkel and Jack Napoli, who created the original, and the name of the company I founded. The book is called MEDDICC and it covers all three versions, because the letters matter less than the questions behind them.

The question MEDDICC answers: is this deal real, and who else is in it?

The mistake is arguing about the acronym instead of running it. I have watched sales leaders spend a whole offsite debating whether they are a MEDDIC team or a MEDDICC team. Nobody at the offsite could name the Economic Buyer on their three biggest deals. Pick a version, write the questions down, and ask them on every deal every week.

How I use it. MEDDICC is binary. You either use it on every opportunity or you do not use it at all, and the teams that half-use it get the worst of both: the admin without the insight. The teams that go all in get a forecast they can stand behind and a pipeline where the weak deals are known early enough to fix or kill. Go all in or leave it alone.

### MEDDPICC
URL: https://andywhyte.com/glossary/meddpicc/

MEDDPICC is the eight-part version of the MEDDIC qualification framework, adding Paper Process and Competition so a deal is qualified all the way to signature.

MEDDPICC is the full version. Metrics, Economic Buyer, Decision Criteria, Decision Process, Paper Process, Implicate the Pain, Champion, Competition. The P is the one people notice, and it is there because the gap between a verbal yes and a signed contract is where quarters go to die. Legal, procurement, security and signature authority were always part of the deal. MEDDPICC made them part of the qualification.

The question MEDDPICC answers is bigger than the other two: is this deal real, can it actually close, by when, and what would stop it?

The mistake is treating it as a form. I have seen CRMs with eight mandatory MEDDPICC fields and a forecast that was still fiction, because the fields were filled in by the seller on a Friday afternoon from memory and nobody ever inspected them. The letters are questions, and the answers have to come from the customer. If the customer has not said it, you do not know it. You are guessing, and guessing is not qualification.

How I use it. MEDDPICC is what I teach, and it is the methodology the MEDDICC Masterclass has taken more than 35,000 graduates through. I use it in two directions. Downwards, into a deal: where are we strong, where are we weak, and what is the next action that changes a weak letter? Upwards, into a forecast: a deal with no Economic Buyer, no Metrics and no Paper Process mapped does not go in commit, whatever the rep's gut says. And one rule above all. People sometimes add a third C for Compelling Event. Do not. Implicated Pain, agreed Metrics and a real Champion produce the urgency. Bolting on a letter does not.

### Coach
URL: https://andywhyte.com/glossary/coach/

A Coach is a contact inside the customer who gives you information and guidance but lacks the power, vested interest or will to sell your deal internally.

A Coach is the person in the account who helps you. They take your calls, tell you who matters, warn you when the mood changes and explain the politics. What they do not do is sell for you. Either they lack the power and influence to move the decision, or they have no personal stake in the outcome, or both. They want you to win in the way a friend wants you to win. They are not going to put their own neck on the line to make it happen.

The question a Coach helps you answer is: what is really going on in there? The question they cannot answer is: who is going to make this happen when I am not there?

The mistake is the oldest one in enterprise sales, and I have made it. You mislabel a Coach as a Champion because the relationship feels strong. Then you forecast the deal on the strength of that relationship. Then the deal stalls in a meeting your Coach could not get into, and the best they can offer is an apology and a summary. Both are useful. Neither closes anything.

How I use it. I value Coaches and I keep them, because the intelligence they give is real. But I never let a Coach stand in the Champion slot of my qualification. The test is behaviour. Ask them to get you in front of the Economic Buyer. A Champion finds a way. A Coach tells you why it is difficult right now. If every senior contact in a deal turns out to be a Coach, I have a deal with information and no engine. That is a deal I build a Champion in, fast, or qualify out of.

### Compelling Event
URL: https://andywhyte.com/glossary/compelling-event/

A Compelling Event is a dated reason, with real consequences, why the customer must act now, built from implicated pain and agreed Metrics rather than the seller's quarter end.

A Compelling Event is something with a date and a cost on the customer's side of the table. A contract expiring. A regulation landing in April. A product launch that fails without the capability you sell. A new CFO who has told the team the number must move by Q3. If the date passes and nothing bad happens to them, it was not compelling. It was a preference.

The question it answers is the one that quietly kills more deals than any competitor: why now?

The mistake is on both sides of the desk. Sellers think a discount that expires on Friday is a Compelling Event. It is not, and customers know it, which is why they call you on the following Tuesday to ask if it is still available. The other mistake is adding a C to the acronym. Some people run MEDDPICCC with a third C for Compelling Event. My view is that this tells the world their understanding of the framework is shallow. The urgency is already in there. Implicated Pain plus agreed Metrics plus a Champion who owns the outcome gives you a customer who needs to move. You do not need a ninth letter. You need to do the other eight properly.

How I use it. Urgency is an emotion, and you cannot email an emotion. So I do not try to manufacture a Compelling Event with pressure. I look for the one that already exists in the customer's world, and if there is none, I help the Champion build one out of the consequences of doing nothing, with a date on it. If there is no date and no consequence, "later" wins every time, and I would rather plan for that than forecast against it.

### Qualifying Out
URL: https://andywhyte.com/glossary/qualifying-out/

Qualifying out is the deliberate decision to stop pursuing an opportunity that fails qualification, so your time goes to deals you can actually win.

Qualifying out is walking away on purpose. You have run the deal through MEDDPICC, you have found that there is no Economic Buyer access, no Champion, no Metrics anyone has agreed to, or no reason to act this year, and you have decided that your time is worth more somewhere else. It is a decision, with a reason you can state out loud, and it is one of the strongest moves a seller can make.

The question it answers: should we even be in this deal?

The mistake is believing that more pipeline is always better. It is not. A pipeline full of deals that will never close costs you the deals that would have. Every hour on a no-hope opportunity is an hour not spent building a Champion in a real one. The other mistake is softer and more common: the seller knows the deal is dead and keeps it alive in the CRM because killing it feels like admitting failure. So it sits there, ageing, propping up a coverage number that everyone upstairs is relying on.

How I use it. Nobody regrets qualifying out. I coined that line years ago to give sellers permission, and I have yet to find the exception. One of two things happens when you qualify out. Either you were right, the opportunity was not worth it, and you have your time back. Or the act of walking away corrects the customer's behaviour. The Economic Buyer who would not meet you suddenly has a slot on Thursday. The Champion who was a Coach finds some power. Either way you win. Carry on pretending and you lose slowly, which is the most expensive way to lose.

### Champion Test
URL: https://andywhyte.com/glossary/champion-test/

The Champion Test checks whether a contact has power and influence, a vested interest in your success, and will act on your behalf when asked.

The Champion Test is how you find out whether the name in your Champion field deserves to be there. It has two halves. First, the three criteria: do they have power and influence, do they have a personal stake in you winning, and are they actively selling for you? Second, and this is the half most sellers skip, you ask them to prove it. You request something that costs them effort or political capital and you watch what happens.

The question it answers: if I disappeared for a month, would this person keep my deal alive?

The mistake is testing with questions instead of asks. "Would you say you are our Champion?" is a question anyone will say yes to, because it is flattering and free. An ask is different. Can you get me thirty minutes with the Economic Buyer before the end of the month? Can you share the scoring sheet the evaluation team is using? Can you tell me what the Economic Buyer said about us after our last meeting? Each of those costs something. The answers, and more importantly the actions that follow, are the test.

How I use it. I run the test early and I run it again before anything goes into commit. A Champion who passes in month one can fail in month four, because they changed role, lost a fight, or found a bigger project. I keep the bar deliberately high. Liking your product is what a Coach does. The Champion I will forecast on sells it internally when I am not in the room, and the only proof of that is something they did. Pass the test and the deal is forecastable. Fail it and you know your next action.

### Discovery
URL: https://andywhyte.com/glossary/discovery/

Discovery is the ongoing work of finding out a customer's pain, Metrics, people and process, carried on through the whole deal rather than finished in one call.

Discovery is how you earn the right to the rest of the deal. It is the questioning, listening and testing that uncovers what the customer is trying to change, why it matters, what it is worth, who decides and how. Done well, discovery is where every letter of MEDDPICC gets its first real answer. Done badly, it is a forty-minute interrogation from a script, followed by a demo the customer did not ask for.

The question it answers: what is actually true about this customer, as opposed to what we hoped was true when we booked the meeting?

The mistake is treating discovery as a stage. A box between "qualified lead" and "demo" that you tick once and never revisit. Deals change. The Economic Buyer gets replaced. The budget gets cut in half. The Champion's rival takes over the project. If your discovery stopped in week two, your qualification is a photograph of a deal that no longer exists. Discovery never stops. The best sellers I know are still discovering in the contract negotiation.

How I use it. I go into every conversation with a point of view on the customer's business and a short list of what I do not know yet. The point of view earns respect. The list keeps me honest. I ask about consequences more than features, I ask the same question of more than one person, and I write down what the customer said in their words rather than my summary of it. Then I check the deal against MEDDPICC and the gaps tell me what to discover next. If I cannot name a gap, I am not inspecting hard enough.

### Mutual Action Plan
URL: https://andywhyte.com/glossary/mutual-action-plan/

A Mutual Action Plan is a shared, dated document agreed with the customer that lists every step, owner and milestone from today to signature and go-live.

A Mutual Action Plan is the Decision Process and the Paper Process written down in one place, with a date and an owner against every line, and agreed by both sides. It starts today and ends at the outcome the customer cares about, which is rarely the signature. It is the go-live, the first report, the number moving. Working backwards from that date, through legal, procurement, security, the business case, the evaluation and the executive meeting, is what turns a hope into a plan.

The question it answers: what has to happen, by whom, by when, for this customer to get what they want?

The mistake is building it alone. A plan the seller writes and emails to the customer is a close plan with the word "mutual" stuck on the front. The customer did not agree to it, so the dates mean nothing. The second mistake is anchoring it on your close date. Customers do not care about your quarter. Anchor it on their outcome and the close date falls out of the maths, usually earlier than you feared or later than you hoped. Both are useful to know.

How I use it. I build the plan with my Champion, then I get the Economic Buyer to see it, because an executive who has looked at a dated plan with their name on a line has made a small commitment that is hard to walk back. Then it becomes the deal's heartbeat. Every slipped line is a question: why, and what does it mean for the rest? A Mutual Action Plan that nobody on the customer's side has touched in three weeks is telling you something. Listen to it.

### Deal Inspection
URL: https://andywhyte.com/glossary/deal-inspection/

Deal inspection is a leader examining a single opportunity against MEDDPICC to find what is proven, what is assumed and what action changes it.

Deal inspection is what a sales leader does to a deal, as opposed to what a seller says about it. You take one opportunity and you go through it letter by letter. Who is the Economic Buyer and when did we last speak to them? What are the Metrics, in the customer's words? Who is the Champion and what have they done for us? Where is the Paper Process and who owns it? For every answer, one follow-up: how do we know? The point is to separate what has been proven by the customer from what has been assumed by the seller.

The question it answers: is this deal as strong as it looks, and what do we do about the parts that are not?

The mistake is confusing inspection with interrogation. An inspection where the seller leaves feeling attacked teaches them to hide things, and a leader who only hears good news is forecasting blind. The other mistake is inspecting outcomes. "Why did we lose?" is a lagging question. "Why did we have no Champion in week six and still forecast it?" is a leading one, and it is the only one you can coach.

How I use it. I judge the decisions in the deal, not the result. A rep who qualified out of a bad deal made a good decision, even if a competitor later closed it. A rep who won without ever meeting the Economic Buyer got lucky, and luck is not a skill I can scale. Inspection done well is a conversation about the next action, every week, on the deals that matter. The book calls it the deal inspection rhythm. The forecast you can stand behind comes out of it.

### Deal Review
URL: https://andywhyte.com/glossary/deal-review/

A deal review is the regular meeting where a seller and their leader inspect live opportunities, agree what is real and decide the next actions.

A deal review is the meeting. Deal inspection is what should happen inside it. A good deal review takes a handful of opportunities, runs each through MEDDPICC with the seller, and ends with a short list of actions, owners and dates. A bad deal review takes forty opportunities, asks "where are we with this one?", gets "I'm working it hard" forty times, and ends with everyone agreeing the forecast is fine.

The question it answers: of all the deals in this pipeline, which are real, which are at risk, and what are we doing this week to change that?

The mistake is letting it become a status update. The seller reads out the CRM. The leader nods. Activity is reported as progress: emailed, chased, pushed, nurtured. None of those are MEDDPICC. If a seller cannot articulate the Champion's economic case in three sentences, the deal is not real, and the effort was theatre. The B in B-Player stands for busy, and the deal review is where busy goes to hide. A leader who accepts effort as evidence will get a pipeline full of it.

How I use it. Fewer deals, more depth. I would rather inspect five opportunities properly than skim thirty. I ask the seller to lead with the weakest letter, because the strong ones look after themselves. I judge the quality of the decisions made in the deal, not the colour of the stage. And I keep the actions. A deal review that produces no actions was a meeting about a meeting. If the same deal turns up three weeks running with the same gap and no movement, that is the signal to qualify out, and it is better to hear it in a review than on the last day of the quarter.

### Forecast Categories
URL: https://andywhyte.com/glossary/forecast-categories/

Forecast categories sort open deals by confidence, typically commit, best case and pipeline, so a leader can roll up a number they will stand behind.

Forecast categories are the shelves you put deals on. Commit is the shelf you would bet your job on: the deals that will close in the period unless something unforeseeable happens. Best case is the shelf of deals that could close in the period if the things still outstanding go your way. Pipeline is everything else that is qualified and real but not yet close enough to call. The names matter less than the rule for what goes on each shelf.

The question they answer: what number can this team put in front of the board and defend?

The mistake is letting gut feel decide the shelf. A seller puts a deal in commit because they like the Champion, or because the quarter needs it, or because they put it there last month and moving it would prompt a conversation. Then the leader rolls up a number built on forty feelings and calls it a forecast. The miss, when it comes, is treated as bad luck. It was not luck. It was a decision, made without evidence, and it should be judged as one.

How I use it. Each category has an evidence test, and the evidence is MEDDPICC. Nothing goes into commit without a Champion who has passed the test, an Economic Buyer who has engaged, Metrics the customer has agreed, and a Paper Process that physically fits the dates. Best case can have a gap, as long as the gap is named and there is an action against it. The categories then stop being opinions and start being leading indicators. A commit deal with no Economic Buyer is a contradiction in terms, and I would rather see it moved than wait for the quarter to move it for me.

### Leading and Lagging Indicators
URL: https://andywhyte.com/glossary/leading-and-lagging-indicators/

Leading indicators are the behaviours and deal conditions that predict a result, while lagging indicators such as revenue and quota attainment report a result that has already happened.

A lagging indicator is a result. Bookings, quota attainment, win rate, churn. By the time you can read it, the work that produced it is finished, and so is your chance to change it. A leading indicator is something that happens earlier and predicts the lagging one. Economic Buyer meetings held. Champions who have passed the test. Metrics agreed in the customer's words. Discovery calls where the consequence of doing nothing was named. Pipeline created from accounts you chose rather than accounts that found you.

The question they answer: what should I be looking at today to know what the quarter will look like in ninety days?

The mistake is running the team on the lagging number. Every sales leader has a dashboard with attainment at the top, and most coaching conversations start there. "You are at 40%." The rep already knew. You cannot coach a lagging indicator. The number is a verdict on decisions made two months ago, and no amount of talking about it changes a single one of them. Leaders who manage this way end up shouting at the scoreboard.

How I use it. I pick a small number of leading indicators that I know produce the result, and I inspect those relentlessly. For most teams I have led, that meant the quality of MEDDPICC on the top deals, the number of Economic Buyer conversations in a month, and how much new pipeline carried a real Champion. Coach those and the lagging number follows, with a lag you can predict. Ignore them and the quarter will tell you how it went, long after you could have done anything about it.

### A, B and C Players
URL: https://andywhyte.com/glossary/a-b-c-players/

A Players are accountable to outcomes, B Players are busy and focused on optics, and a C Player is a label that should not exist on any serious team.

A Players are uncomfortable being comfortable. They are driven by an unreasonable demand to reach their own potential, they measure themselves on impact, and they are suspicious of ease. The A stands for accountable. B Players focus on optics. They avoid clarity, dodge accountability and manage perception rather than create value. The B stands for busy. And a C Player? There is no such thing. Or at least there should not be. Professional sports teams have no room for them, and neither does your go-to-market team.

The question this answers for a leader: who on this team is actually producing, and where should my time go?

The mistake is spending leadership time in the wrong place. Profile a team honestly and you get three groups. A Players. B+ Players, who have the potential to be an A or are out of form. And B- Players, who do not have the potential. Most leaders spend a disproportionate amount of their week on the B- group, and the A Players, who would grow fastest with that attention, get left to get on with it. The other mistake is forgetting that A is relative to the role and subject to form. A first-year AE can be an A Player. A ten-year veteran can lose their A game for a quarter.

How I use it. I look for effort displayed as evidence. The AE with 27 open opportunities, all yellow or red, defending each one with "I'm working it hard", is the B-Player tell. It is not laziness. It is activity standing in for outcomes. The work is legible now, so busyness hides nothing. I coach to the outcome, I remove the barriers that slow A Players down, and I am honest with myself that the barrier is sometimes a B- Player.

### Sales Kickoff
URL: https://andywhyte.com/glossary/sales-kickoff/

A sales kickoff, or SKO, is the annual event where a sales organisation aligns on strategy, targets, product and methodology for the year ahead.

A sales kickoff is the one time in the year the whole revenue team is in a room together. Strategy, targets, new products, the comp plan, the methodology, and usually a keynote speaker, an awards dinner and a hangover. I have sat through a lot of them, on both sides of the stage, and the good ones are easy to spot. They change what people do on the Monday after.

The question an SKO should answer: what are we doing differently this year, and does every seller leave knowing their part in it?

The mistake is treating the kickoff as the message. Leaders stand up and talk about urgency, about hunger, about a big year. Then everyone flies home and the pipeline looks exactly as it did in December. Urgency is an emotion, not a message. You cannot tell a team to be urgent from a stage, and you cannot email it to them afterwards. It is built from how leaders behave in the weeks that follow: consistent, truthful, clear about consequences and commitments. A kickoff that is not followed by that behaviour was a party with slides.

How I use it. I treat SKO as the launch of an operating rhythm rather than the rhythm itself. If MEDDPICC is being introduced or sharpened, the kickoff is where the whole team hears the same definitions, works real deals in the room, and watches the leadership team run a deal inspection live, including the uncomfortable bits. Then the deal reviews start the following week and do not stop. The two sessions I would never cut: the A Players telling the room what they actually did last year, and the leadership team saying what they got wrong. Both are more useful than the keynote. Including mine.
